# RequestFox: the full text of every page

Version 2.5.0, site updated 2026-11-19. The short guide is https://requestfox.accessisight.com/llms.txt.

# See which API call Failed.

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/

No login, works offline. RequestFox is a free API tester and network monitor in a side panel for Chrome, Edge and Firefox. It records every call your web app makes, flags the broken ones the moment they happen, and lets you replay, mock and test them.

Add to Chrome, free
Add to Firefox

No account. Nothing is sent to us. No AI inside.

## Where RequestFox stands

Each of these API testing tools is the right pick for some job. Pick RequestFox when you're testing a web app and want its API problems found for you, the moment they happen.

- DevTools Network: Lists every request. You do the judging.

- Postman, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch: Send the requests you type.

- RequestFox: Records what your app actually sends, says what broke, and sends yours too.

### Which tool for which job

- Testing a web app and want problems found for you

RequestFox. It records the calls as you click, flags what failed, dragged, fired twice or broke inside a 200 OK, and keeps every session.

- A raw look at everything one page load does

The DevTools Network panel. Built into the browser, and you do the filtering and reading. RequestFox vs DevTools

- Designing, documenting and sharing APIs across a team

Postman or Insomnia. RequestFox imports from both and exports back to both. RequestFox vs Postman · RequestFox vs Insomnia

- Requests kept as plain files in Git, next to the code

Bruno. In Chrome, RequestFox can keep a collection in a linked folder as files too. RequestFox vs Bruno

- An open-source client on the web you can host yourself

Hoppscotch. RequestFox has nothing to host: there's no server. RequestFox vs Hoppscotch

### Where RequestFox falls short

- It sees what a browser tab sends. Mobile and desktop apps need a proxy tool such as HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman or Charles.

- There's no team workspace or cloud sync, by design. You share work as files: collections, sessions, HAR and reports.

- Scripts run in Chrome only: Firefox doesn't let extensions run code typed at runtime.

- No native gRPC or MQTT client (gRPC-Web and Connect only).

Every comparison, with sources

## Every problem, named in plain words

Calls are judged as they finish. Pick a flag to read what the panel tells you about it.

Flag
Failed
Slow
GraphQL error
Token expired
Schema changed
Flaky ×3

POST /api/orders 500 412 ms

Why is this flagged?

The server failed while answering (a 5xx status).

What to do: Look at the server's logs for this moment; Replay sends the same request again to see if it repeats.

GET /api/search?q=boots 200 3.1 s

Why is this flagged?

The response took longer than your slow limit.

What to do: Timing in Details shows where the time went; the limit is in Settings.

POST /graphql 200 96 ms

Why is this flagged?

The response says the call failed, although its HTTP status is OK.

What to do: Read the error in the response: the status alone hides this failure.

GET /api/me 401 54 ms

Why is this flagged?

The call was refused and the token it sent had already expired.

What to do: Sign in again or refresh the token, then send the call again.

GET /api/cart 200 120 ms

Why is this flagged?

The response's shape (its fields and their types) is not what this call returned before.

What to do: Open the shape diff on the card to see what changed.

GET /api/stock/42 503 230 ms

Why is this flagged?

This call failed in some recorded sessions and passed in others.

What to do: Compare a failing and a passing response in History.

Every flag RequestFox raises

A failed call opened: its response, with Replay one click away.

## From the flag to the fix

01 Replay

### Replay it, or edit it first

Send any recorded call again as it was, or change it in Compose. Environments, {{variables}}, OAuth 2.0 with device code, OAuth 1.0a, JWT Bearer and AWS Signature v4 are built in, and several requests can stay open at once.

Keep saved examples and notes on requests and collections. A cookie jar you switch on per site carries a sign-in to your next sends, and the WebSocket client has a Socket.IO mode.

How to replay and edit a request

02 Mock

### Mock it, break it, slow it

Open a call and press Mock: its real status and body are there to change. Press Mock it, reload the page, and the page gets your response. A rule can also make a call fail, slow it down or pause it, without touching the backend. Rule sets and mock sets stay on when you want them to.

In Chrome you can also slow the whole tab, or rewrite a request or response with a script. Calls you changed carry a Mocked or Simulated label, so nobody mistakes them for real bugs.

How to mock an API response

03 Test

### Check it, then run the same checks in CI

Add checks to an endpoint: status, time, fields, headers or a JSON Schema, and chain saved requests into suites. The downloadable command-line tool runs them in your pipeline and fails the build when a check fails. You also get advice on caching and compression, and a check that a response stays the same as last time.

Collections come in from Postman, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch and Thunder Client, OpenAPI 3, Swagger 2, WSDL, HAR and cURL. They go back out as Postman collections, collections for Bruno, Insomnia and Hoppscotch, OpenAPI 3.0, an API docs page, code in 15 languages, or Playwright, Cypress, k6, JMeter, Gatling and Locust scripts.

How to run your API checks in CI

$ node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --config requestfox.config.json
✓ GET /api/me — status = 200 (actual: 200)
✓ GET /api/cart — status = 200 (actual: 200)
✓ GET /api/search?q=boots — status = 200 (actual: 200)
✖ GET /api/search?q=boots — latency < 800ms (actual: 1305) [RF-CHECK-LATENCY]
✖ POST /api/orders — status = 200 (actual: 500) [RF-CHECK-STATUS]

5 assertion(s) checked.

A real run of the command-line tool against a small test shop API: two checks fail, so it exits with 1 and the pipeline stops.

04 AI tools

### Test your AI tools, with no AI inside

RequestFox runs no AI model. It tests the AI tools you build: Compose connects to an MCP server and calls its tools, and a call to a language-model API shows the model, the token counts the response gives, the stop reason and the time.

With MCP control switched on (it's off by default), an AI agent on your own computer can record, replay and mock through RequestFox. Every send and replay waits for your click.

How MCP control stays safe

Controlled by a local MCP client

Allow this MCP action?

A local MCP client asks for this: Send POST shop.example.com/api/orders. Nothing happens unless you allow it.

CancelAllow

## Press Alt Shift S, then use your app.

Every fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket frame and server-sent event appears the moment it starts, across tabs, frames and pop-ups, even calls a service worker answers.

Every call is tied to the click or form submit that caused it, and each session stays in History so you can compare it with the next.

On a Mac, it's Option Shift S. Or open the side panel and press Start. How to record API calls, step by step

Written for QA testers, frontend developers and API developers. All guides, including checking calls against an OpenAPI spec.

## Facts

It reads collections from 5 other API apps, writes code in 15 languages, turns a recording into tests for 6 tools, and speaks 14 languages. It costs nothing.

- Works in: Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge (side panel), Mozilla Firefox (sidebar)

- Price: Free, no paid tier

- Account: None

- Where your data lives: In your browser. There is no RequestFox server and no analytics.

- Secrets: Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields redacted by default

- Interface languages: 14

- Version: 2.5.0, what changed

- Source code: MIT licence; repository not public

- Made by: AccessiSight

## Questions

### Is RequestFox free?

Yes. RequestFox is free, and our promise is written here: nothing you can use for free today will be put behind a paywall later. It has no ads, no account and no paid tier.

### Does RequestFox send my data anywhere?

No. Everything RequestFox records stays in your browser's storage on your device. There is no RequestFox server, no analytics and no account. Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields are redacted by default in everything RequestFox keeps, logs or exports (Compose shows the response to your own request as it came; its Recent list keeps your last 100 sends, redacted, on this device until you press Clear), and site access is asked for only when you press Start, or, for the sites involved, when you send from Compose or run a test suite with nothing recording.

### Does RequestFox use AI?

No. RequestFox runs no AI model. It can test the AI tools you build: MCP servers, and the calls a page makes to a language-model API. With MCP control switched on, which is off by default, an AI agent on your own computer can drive it, and every send waits for your click.

### Is there a free Postman alternative that runs in the browser?

RequestFox is a free browser extension that composes and sends requests with environments, {{variables}}, auth helpers including OAuth 2.0 and saved collections, imports Postman, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch and Thunder Client collections, and exports Postman collections and collections for Bruno, Insomnia and Hoppscotch. Unlike a standalone client it also records the calls your web app really makes. It has no cloud workspace or team sync.

### How is RequestFox different from the DevTools Network panel?

DevTools shows every request and leaves the judging to you. RequestFox flags failed, slow, duplicate and retried calls as they happen, ties each one to the click that caused it, checks your per-endpoint rules, and keeps every session so you can compare today's run with yesterday's. DevTools is better for a raw, live view of everything a page loads.

More questions and answers

# About RequestFox and AccessiSight

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/about.html

RequestFox is a free API tester and network monitor for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, made by AccessiSight. It runs in your browser: there is no RequestFox server, no account and no analytics, and nothing you record is sent to us.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

## What RequestFox is

It's a side panel in Chrome and Edge and a sidebar in Firefox. While you use the web app you're testing, it records every API call the app makes and flags the ones that failed, dragged, fired twice or broke inside a 200 OK. Each flag says what went wrong in plain words, and what to do next.

The same panel is also an API client, a way to mock or break a call without touching the backend, a set of checks you can run in CI with its downloadable command-line tool, and a tester for the AI tools you build. Everything it does

## Who makes it

RequestFox is made and published by AccessiSight, the RequestFox team. The same team writes the comparison pages on this site. Every fact they state about another tool comes from that tool's own documentation, linked and dated on each page. Every comparison, with sources

## Why it is free

RequestFox is free, and we put the promise in writing: nothing you can use for free today will go behind a paywall later. There are no ads, no account and no paid tier.

## Where your data lives

Everything RequestFox records stays in your browser's storage on your device. There is no RequestFox server, no analytics and no account. Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields are redacted by default in everything RequestFox keeps, logs or exports. Requests you send yourself go to the servers you chose, and nowhere else.

The privacy policy, in full

## How it is built

- No AI inside: RequestFox runs no AI model and gives nothing you record, type or send to any AI service.

- The extension ships no third-party code and takes no plugins.

- It works in Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge and Mozilla Firefox, in 14 interface languages.

- It is free. Its code is MIT-licensed and ships readable inside the extension, so you can check it yourself; the source repository is not public.

What changed in each version

## Questions and bugs

Something not working? Write to us at the address in section 8 of the privacy policy and say which browser and version, or use Help → Report a problem… in the panel: it copies a short text for you to paste, or opens your own mail program, and sends nothing itself. If Help doesn't show it, press All tours first. Have a question about privacy or how the extension behaves? Write to the same address. If RequestFox helps you, a review on the Chrome Web Store or Firefox Add-ons helps others find it.

Found a security problem? Write to the same address with “RequestFox security” in the subject, and you get a reply within 7 days. The address is also in security.txt.

# Which API testing extension should I use?

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/faq.html

Straight answers to the questions people ask about testing APIs in the browser. Where another tool is the better fit, we say so.

Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## Choosing a tool

**What is the best API testing extension for Chrome?**

It depends on the job. To test the API calls a web app makes while you use it, and have failed, slow and duplicate calls flagged for you, use RequestFox. For a raw look at everything one page load does, the built-in DevTools Network panel needs no install. To build and share API collections across a team, Postman is the usual choice; to keep them as files in git, Bruno; for always-on rules that redirect or rewrite traffic, Requestly.

**What is a good API testing add-on for Firefox?**

RequestFox runs in Firefox as a sidebar with the same recording, flags, mocks, checks and exports as in Chrome. Firefox's own Network Monitor is built in and shows every request. In Firefox, pre-request and post-response scripts, and rewriting a request or response with a script, don't run (Firefox does not let extensions run code typed at runtime; chaining values between requests still works). One small difference: clicking a RequestFox notification opens the sidebar in the window you are looking at, which may not be the one being recorded.

**Is there a free Postman alternative that runs in the browser?**

RequestFox is a free browser extension that composes and sends requests with environments, {{variables}}, auth helpers including OAuth 2.0 and saved collections, imports Postman, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch and Thunder Client collections, and exports Postman collections and collections for Bruno, Insomnia and Hoppscotch. Unlike a standalone client it also records the calls your web app really makes. It has no cloud workspace or team sync.

**How is RequestFox different from the DevTools Network panel?**

DevTools shows every request and leaves the judging to you. RequestFox flags failed, slow, duplicate and retried calls as they happen, ties each one to the click that caused it, checks your per-endpoint rules, and keeps every session so you can compare today's run with yesterday's. DevTools is better for a raw, live view of everything a page loads.

## Finding API bugs

**How do I see every API call a website makes?**

Open DevTools (F12), choose Network, and filter by Fetch/XHR. To keep the list while you click through a whole flow and have problems flagged for you, open the RequestFox side panel, press Start, and use the site: every fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket and server-sent event call is listed the moment it starts.

**How do I find failed, slow or duplicate API calls while testing?**

RequestFox flags them as they happen: every 4xx, 5xx and dropped connection, calls slower than a threshold you set, rapid double-fires and retries. Each flag is tied to the click or form submit that caused it, and failures are explained in plain words. By hand, sort the DevTools Network panel by Status, Time and Name and compare rows.

**How do I catch GraphQL errors that come back as 200 OK?**

GraphQL servers often answer 200 OK with an errors array in the body, so the status column looks fine. Check each response body for a non-empty errors key, and treat it as a failure in your client and tests. RequestFox reads GraphQL and JSON-RPC responses and flags these errors automatically, with the server's own message.

**Why does an API return 401 when the token looks fine?**

Often the access token expired minutes earlier and was never refreshed. The middle part of a JWT is base64url-encoded JSON with an exp time you can compare with the response's Date header. RequestFox decodes the bearer token locally, reading only its times, issuer and audience, and says on the request when an expired token caused the 401 or 403.

**How can I spot N+1 API calls in the browser?**

Look for one path called again and again with only an id changing, like /products/101/reviews, /products/102/reviews, in a short burst. RequestFox turns paths into templates such as /products/{id}/reviews and flags the burst as N+1. The fix is a batch endpoint or including the data in the list response.

**How do I know when an API response changed shape?**

RequestFox remembers the JSON shape each endpoint returned earlier in the session and flags Schema changed when a field is added, removed or changes type, with exactly what differs. For a fixed contract, add a per-endpoint check with a JSON Schema.

## Mocking, exporting and testing

**How do I mock an API response in Chrome without a backend?**

In RequestFox, press Mock on a recorded call's card: the dialog holds that call's real status and body, which you can change, and Mock it returns them, with the call's headers, for the page's fetch and XMLHttpRequest calls. A fault rule can instead make a call fail like a dropped connection, add delay, or pause it so you can edit the request or response. Mocked responses are labelled in the log.

**Can I turn browser traffic into load tests?**

Yes. After a recording, RequestFox's Performance panel turns the recorded endpoints into a runnable k6, JMeter, Gatling or Locust script, with your chosen users, ramp-up and duration, and each endpoint's measured p95 latency as its pass/fail threshold. It can also export end-to-end tests for Playwright or Cypress.

**How do I export network requests as HAR, Postman or OpenAPI?**

RequestFox exports a recorded session as a HAR file, a Postman collection, an OpenAPI 3.0 spec built from the calls, CSV, session JSON or a self-contained HTML report. Your saved collections export for Bruno, Insomnia or Hoppscotch, or as one API docs page (Export docs). It also copies any single request as code in 15 languages, cURL for bash and Windows cmd included. Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields are redacted by default.

**Can RequestFox send a request to any API?**

While recording, Compose and Replay send through the page you are testing, with its cookies and session. With nothing recording, Compose sends the request itself, without any page's cookies, after the browser asks once for that site. When an API blocks the page's origin (CORS), Compose offers Send from the extension instead, and a Replay is sent again from the extension by itself: no page cookies, marked From extension in the log. Copy as code also turns any request into cURL or another language to run outside the browser.

## Privacy and cost

**Does RequestFox send my data anywhere?**

No. Everything RequestFox records stays in your browser's storage on your device. There is no RequestFox server, no analytics and no account. Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields are redacted by default in everything RequestFox keeps, logs or exports (Compose shows the response to your own request as it came; its Recent list keeps your last 100 sends, redacted, on this device until you press Clear), and site access is asked for only when you press Start, or, for the sites involved, when you send from Compose or run a test suite with nothing recording.

**Is RequestFox free? Is it open source?**

RequestFox is free, and our promise is written here: nothing you can use for free today will be put behind a paywall later. Its code is MIT-licensed and ships readable inside the extension, so you can check it yourself; the source repository is not public. It has no ads, no account and no paid tier.

**Which languages does RequestFox speak?**

The interface is available in 14 languages: English, Arabic (right to left), Chinese (Simplified), French, German, Hindi, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese (Brazil), Russian, Spanish and Turkish. It follows the browser's language, or you can pick one in Settings.

# What the RequestFox API tester does

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/features.html

RequestFox is a free API tester and network monitor for Chrome, Edge and Firefox. It records the API calls a web app makes while you use it, flags the ones that went wrong, and lets you replay, mock, check and export them. All of it runs inside Chrome, Edge or Firefox, with no account and no server.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

The Timeline, one of the panel's views.

## Record every call, the moment it starts

Press Start (or Alt Shift S) and use your app. RequestFox lists fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket frames and server-sent events across tabs, iframes and pop-ups, including calls a service worker answers without the network.

- A call shows as soon as it starts and turns Slow live if it drags; its finished card replaces it.

- Live streams: server-sent events, NDJSON and token streams, read with fetch, XMLHttpRequest or EventSource, stay open as rows that fill as events arrive. RequestFox keeps the newest ones within the body limit, and flags error events, a missing end marker and long pauses. A page's gRPC-Web or Connect server stream is kept the same way.

- The log can be a table: one line per call, sorted by a click on a heading, with columns that read a value out of each JSON response (data.items.length), a Group by host view and a session Overview (calls, errors, slow calls, status families, the slowest five, hosts). A 5,000-call log only draws the rows on screen.

- Table columns: Add column reads one value from each JSON response by a path (data.items.length, $.user.id) and offers the paths of a response as suggestions. Columns shows or hides the table's own columns, takes up to four response columns, and puts them in the order you want (drag a heading, or use the arrows in the dialog). The choice is saved for the site.

- The Overview has Copy as Markdown for a bug report (calls named by host and path only: no query string, headers or bodies) and a Calls over time bar chart, with the busiest stretch also written in words.

- With two or more browser windows open, Start can also record the same site in your other windows. Show page files (Settings, off by default) lists the page's own scripts, styles, images and fonts too, each with a badge, and never raises an alert for them.

- Each call is tied to the click or form submit that caused it.

- Every session goes to History, to reopen, search and compare with another run.

- Search takes free text and tokens such as status:500, host:api.example.com and path:/users/:id; a leading - leaves matches out.

## Problems flagged for you

These are the panel's own labels. Open a flagged call and it says what happened in plain words.

- Failed refused, timed out, or a 4xx/5xx response

- Slow past the slow threshold you set

- Duplicate · after 140 ms the same call fired twice in a moment

- Retry · after 900 ms sent again after it failed

- One call per item N+1: one call per id in a quick burst

- GraphQL error an error inside a 200 OK

- RPC error a JSON-RPC error inside a 200 OK

- Token expired a 401 caused by an expired JWT

- Schema changed the response's JSON shape changed

- Spec mismatch the call breaks your linked OpenAPI spec

- Check failed one of your checks failed

- Security a passive finding, such as a token in a URL

## Inspect without leaving the page

Each call opens to its headers, body and Details: the timing split (DNS, connect, TLS, waiting, download), the HTTP version, bytes on the wire, and the page functions that made the call.

- JSON responses read as a tree you can filter, with a value's path one click away.

- A web address in a response is a link that opens a new GET request in Compose, and so is an address or a path from the site's root in the JSON tree (Open as request). On the same site the call's headers come along (not the ones redaction hid); to another site, none do.

- Hex shows any response as bytes (offset, hex and ASCII; a longer response shows 32 KB and says so), with Copy hex and Copy as base64.

- A JSON response that is a list of objects offers Table beside Tree: the first six columns, a column picker, 100 rows at a time, sort by a heading, and Copy as CSV (a text a spreadsheet would run as a formula is written as text).

- The Timeline puts every call on a time ruler; Performance lists the heaviest endpoints.

- GraphQL calls are checked against a schema you load, and so are their responses: a wrong type, a null in a non-null field or a missing field is named by its place in the response. A custom scalar that declares @specifiedBy is checked by it (a date-time, UUID, URL or email address); one that does not takes any value. Every flagged call carries a stable finding code (such as RF-FAILED-5XX) and a "Why is this flagged?" explanation, offline.

- gRPC-Web and Connect responses are read as fields once you load your .proto files (RequestFox's own parser), and by field number without them.

- SOAP and XML: import a WSDL (a WSDL split over several files is followed), read an XML response as a tree, and add XPath checks (XPath 1.0 subset, our own reader).

- A call to an LLM API (OpenAI-style, Anthropic or Gemini) shows the model, the token counts and the stop reason its own response gives. Nothing is estimated, and no cost is shown.

A JSON response as a tree.

## Compose, replay and send

Replay any recorded call, or change it first with Edit and send again… in its ··· menu. Compose builds requests from scratch with Params, Headers, raw, form or multipart bodies, environments and {{variables}}, secret variables kept encrypted, and saved collections. Up to five requests stay open at once as chips above the URL, each with its own form and response, and they come back when the panel opens again (typed secrets are never written to disk).

- Auth: Basic, Bearer, API key, Digest, OAuth 2.0 (browser sign-in with PKCE, device code, client credentials, refresh token, password), OpenID Connect discovery, OAuth 1.0a (HMAC, RSA and PLAINTEXT signatures), JWT Bearer signing (HS, RS and ES algorithms), AWS Signature v4 and an HMAC preset.

- Save a response as an example, and keep notes on requests, collections and folders. The QUERY method (a safe request with a body) is in every method list.

- A cookie jar, per site and off until you turn it on, keeps the cookies a site sets so a sign-in carries to your next sends. It never touches the browser's own cookies, and cookie values never go into an export or the log. Importing the browser's cookies for a site is the one step that asks for an optional permission.

- While recording, a send goes through the page with its cookies; with nothing recording it goes from the extension itself, without any page's cookies.

- A GraphQL subscription sent from Compose opens a WebSocket (graphql-transport-ws or the older graphql-ws) and lists the events live, each checked against the schema you loaded. Send reads Stop meanwhile. Headers and auth go with the handshake (the browser may ask you to allow RequestFox on that site) and in the connection's connection_init payload. Nothing is recorded or kept.

- A collection or folder can pin a Default environment: sending one of its saved requests, or opening it in Compose, switches to that environment. One you pick by hand is kept.

- A WebSocket client connects to any ws:// or wss:// server, with a Socket.IO mode; recorded Socket.IO frames read as events and their arguments.

- An MCP server tester: connect to an MCP server over Streamable HTTP, list its tools, resources and prompts, and call one from a form built from its schema. It only sends the requests you pick and shows the responses.

- Copy any request as code in 15 languages, cURL for bash and Windows cmd included.

- Environments can inherit from a parent, and a .env file imports as an environment (credential-like values go to the encrypted vault).

Import from Postman, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch, Thunder Client, OpenAPI 3, Swagger 2, HAR and cURL, from a file, several files or a whole folder at once (batch import, with one summary of what happened to each file), or from a URL (Import from URL: the browser asks for access to that one site). How to replay and edit a request.

## Mocks and faults

Make an endpoint fail, slow down, pause for editing, or return the response you choose, with no backend change. Press Mock on any recorded call: its dialog holds the real status and body, to change before you press Mock it. The card then says Mocked, with a menu to edit the response, keep it on without recording, or turn it off.

- Rule sets and mock sets stay on with nothing recording: switch one on and its header, URL or mock rules apply to the sites it names in every tab, until you switch it off. A chip under the top bar says what is on. Each is one JSON file to share.

- In Chrome, rewrite the request or the response with a script: sign a header, add a field to every body, or change what the page gets back. In Chrome and Firefox, WebSocket message rules drop or change a socket's text messages by text or a JSON field.

- In Chrome, Slow down the whole tab (Slow 3G, Fast 3G, 4G, offline or your own numbers) through the browser's debugger. It is optional, asks once, and Chrome then shows its own "started debugging this browser" bar. Firefox has no such API, so it offers each rule's Slow and Throttle modes instead. DevTools throttles with nothing to allow.

Mock or break an endpoint, in Settings.

How to mock an API response.

## Checks, contracts and suites

Add pass/fail checks to an endpoint on status, time, fields, headers or a JSON Schema, or a check that a response stays the same as last time. Advice on caching and compression points out a large text response sent uncompressed, or the same response downloaded again with nothing a cache could use. Link an OpenAPI spec and every call is checked against it, with coverage of the operations seen. Chain saved requests into suites, with pass or fail per step and data-driven runs. Run options on a suite set a wait between steps (0 to 60 s, for an API that rate-limits), a number of runs (1 to 100) and stop at the first failure; Export as CI config carries them to requestfox-ci run, whose --delay-ms, --bail and --iterations override them.

A call that breaks the linked OpenAPI spec.

How to check API calls against OpenAPI.

## MCP control: let a local agent drive RequestFox

An AI agent that you run on your own computer can use RequestFox through its own MCP server. RequestFox itself runs no AI model; it only answers the tool calls an agent sends it. It is off by default.

- In Settings, Sign-in, cookies & connections, MCP control, turn on Let a local MCP client control RequestFox and press Download the CLI: one file, Node 18 or newer, with the MCP server inside. Start it with node requestfox-ci.mjs mcp --http 3333 --control, give your agent the address and the token it prints, type the port and the one-time pairing code into RequestFox, and press Connect. The browser asks for access to http://127.0.0.1 only.

- 21 more tools while connected: start and stop recording, list calls with the panel's search syntax, read one call, replay it, send a request from Compose, create, change and delete mock and fail rules, switch rule sets and mock sets on or off, run saved requests and suites, export a HAR, report or docs page, clear the log and delete a collection. The whole-tab throttle is Chrome only.

- Pairing code: 10 letters and digits, good once and for 10 minutes, one try a second, replaced after 5 wrong ones. The session key stays in memory, and a session ends after 8 hours, when you press Disconnect, or when you close the panel or quit the browser.

- Local only: the extension connects out to 127.0.0.1, and the server refuses web pages and DNS-rebinding hosts. A chip under the top bar says Controlled by a local MCP client. Every action is listed under MCP actions, and at most 120 tool calls run a minute.

- Your click: sending or replaying a request (the host is shown), deleting a rule, changing a rule you made, clearing the log and deleting a collection each wait for you. So does a saved request or suite that changes data.

- What it cannot reach: no tool reads the cookie jar, the vault, secret variables or OAuth tokens. A request with {{variables}} is refused. Responses are redacted as exports are.

## Export evidence and tests

Export a session as a self-contained HTML report, HAR, CSV, session JSON, a Postman collection or an OpenAPI 3.0 spec built from the calls. Export your saved collections for Bruno, Insomnia or Hoppscotch (passwords, tokens and keys become empty variables to fill in), or as one API docs page (Export docs) with no script and no outside link. Open a GitHub or Linear issue with the repro filled in. Turn a recording into tests:

- Playwright
- Cypress
- k6
- JMeter
- Gatling
- Locust

Run the same checks in CI with the command-line tool you download from the panel; it can also make negative tests from an OpenAPI spec (probe) and serve a mock API from one (mock). The CLI can send over HTTP/2 (--http2, no quiet fall-back to HTTP/1.1), write the docs page (docs), say why a finding is flagged (explain) and fail only on new findings (--baseline). How to run API checks in CI.

## Private by design

No account, no server, no analytics. Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields are redacted in everything you view or export, and site access is asked for when you press Start. Read the privacy policy.

## What it does not do

- It sees what a browser tab sends. Mobile and desktop apps need a proxy tool such as HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman or Charles.

- No team workspace or cloud sync, by design. Share work as files: collections, sessions, HAR and reports.

- Pre-request and post-response scripts, and rewriting a request or response with a script, run in Chrome only; Firefox does not let extensions run code typed at runtime. Chaining values between requests works in both.

- No native gRPC or MQTT client: gRPC-Web and Connect work from a browser; client and bidirectional streams cannot be sent from one.

- RequestFox contains no AI model and no AI code. The MCP server tester and the LLM call view only test and inspect other services, and MCP control only answers an agent you run yourself. MCP servers that run as a local program (stdio) are out of a browser's reach.

- It is free. Its code is MIT-licensed and ships readable inside the extension, so you can check it yourself; the source repository is not public.

## See it on your own app.

Free, in Chrome, Edge and Firefox.

Add to Chrome, free
Add to Firefox

# The RequestFox command line

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/cli.html

requestfox-ci.mjs is RequestFox's command line: one file with no dependencies, for Node 18 or newer, that you download from the panel. Run node requestfox-ci.mjs <command> in a terminal or a CI job. It exits 0 when everything passed, 1 when a check or finding failed, and 2 when the command could not run.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

## Get the file

The command line ships inside the extension, so there is nothing to install and its version is the extension's. Two buttons save it:

- From a test suite: on the suite's card choose ··· → Export as CI config, then press Download the CLI in the dialog. You get requestfox.config.json and requestfox-ci.mjs. The CI guide goes through it step by step.

- From Settings → Sign-in, cookies & connections → MCP control: press Download the CLI.

Put the file next to your config and check that it runs:

node requestfox-ci.mjs --version

It prints requestfox-ci 2.5.0.

## Commands

Twelve commands. Each line shows the flags it needs; node requestfox-ci.mjs <command> --help prints all of its flags.

|

| Command | What it does

| assert --config <file> | Sends every request in the config for real and checks every rule. A step with no check fails when the response is 4xx or 5xx.

| diff --config <file> | Compares each response's shape with a saved baseline. --save-baseline writes the baseline first.

| run <folder> | Runs a workspace folder (the one RequestFox keeps for git) or a workspace.json, suite by suite. --suite and --env pick one suite and one environment.

| loadtest --config <file> | Sends the config's requests from many virtual users (--vus 10 --duration 30s), at a fixed rate (--rate 50), or in steps until the API slows down (--find-breakpoint). Load-test only a system you own or have permission to test.

| merge-results --file <file> --file <file> | Combines loadtest --json files written on several machines into one result.

| conform --spec <file> --session <file> | Checks a recorded session or HAR against an OpenAPI spec, or against a GraphQL schema with --graphql-schema. Exit 1 on a mismatch or a call that is not in the spec. How.

| probe --spec <file> --base <address> | Makes tests from an OpenAPI spec and sends them: each case breaks one rule, and your API must refuse it with a 4xx. Careful by default: this computer only, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and QUERY only, 5 requests a second and at most 200 cases, unless you allow more.

| mock --spec <file> | A local mock server on 127.0.0.1, from a spec, from a recorded session (--session) or from a workspace's saved examples (--workspace). --dynamic varies the responses; --seed 42 repeats them.

| docs --workspace <folder> --out docs.html | Your saved collections as one HTML page of API docs, with no request sent. Passwords, tokens and keys become {{variables}}.

| device-login --device-url <address> --token-url <address> --client-id <id> | OAuth 2.0 device code sign-in: shows the page and the code, waits for you to approve, and prints the access token.

| explain <code> | What a finding code such as RF-SLOW means, why it is flagged and what to do. With no code it lists them all.

| mcp --http <port> --control | RequestFox's MCP server, for an AI tool on this computer, over stdio or, with --http, over HTTP on 127.0.0.1. --control lets the panel pair with it (Settings → MCP control). RequestFox runs no AI model.

## Exit codes

|

| Code | Means

| 0 | Everything passed.

| 1 | A check or a finding failed. A load test fails only on a threshold; with none it exits 0.

| 2 | The command could not run, for example: an unknown flag, a config that does not load, a missing baseline, scripts without --allow-scripts, or an environment variable that is not allowed.

## Environment variables and secrets

A config reads a secret as {{env:NAME}}, so the value stays out of the file. The command must name each variable it may read: add --allow-env NAME (names separated by commas, or the flag again; * allows all), or set REQUESTFOX_ALLOW_ENV=NAME,NAME. Without it the run stops before any request, with exit code 2 and one sentence that names the variable.

node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --config requestfox.config.json --allow-env API_TOKEN

In the log and the JUnit file, values of fields and headers that look like secrets are shown as "hidden".

## The config file

assert, diff and loadtest read requestfox.config.json (--config <file>). A suite card's ··· → Export as CI config writes one; you can also write it by hand. A small one:

{
"baseUrl": "http://localhost:3000",
"requests": [
{ "name": "List users", "method": "GET", "path": "/users" }
],
"assertions": [
{ "pattern": "/users", "type": "status", "op": "=", "value": 200 },
{ "pattern": "/users", "type": "latency", "op": "<", "value": 800 }
]
}

### Top level

|

| Field | What it is

| baseUrl | Required. A full address, like http://localhost:3000. {{env:NAME}} and {{name}} from variables work in it.

| requests | Required for assert and diff: the steps, in order (fields below).

| variables | { "name": "value" }, used as {{name}} in any step.

| data | Rows for a data-driven run, [{ "sku": "A-1" }, ...]: the steps run once per row, each row's fields as {{sku}}.

| dataFile | The same rows from a CSV or JSON file beside the config.

| assertions | The checks (fields below). A step that no check applies to fails on a 4xx or 5xx.

| timeoutMs | Time limit for each request, in ms.

| scriptTimeoutMs | Time limit for each script, in ms.

| delayMs | Wait between steps, 0 to 60000 ms (--delay-ms).

| bail | true: stop at the first failure (--bail).

| iterations | Repeat the whole run 1 to 100 times (--iterations).

| retryCount | Send a step that did not pass again, 0 to 10 times.

| httpErrors | false: a 4xx or 5xx fails a step only through a check.

| bodyErrors | false: an error inside a 2xx response (GraphQL, JSON-RPC) does not fail the step.

| security | false: no security scan of the responses. "securityHeaders": false leaves out the header checks; "securityHeuristics": true adds the guesses.

| failOnSecurity | true: a security finding fails the run.

| baselineFile | Where diff keeps the shapes (by default .requestfox-baseline.json beside the config).

| name | The run's name in the reports.

| loadTest | loadtest's own options (below).

### Each request

|

| Field | What it is

| name | The step's name in the log and the reports.

| method, path | "GET" and "/users/42", added to baseUrl (a full address works too).

| headers | { "Name": "value" }

| body | The body: text, or a JSON value.

| auth | The sign-in an exported suite carries, like { "type": "bearer", ... }.

| extract | Values to save from the response, used as {{name}} by later steps.

| pathVariables | Values for the :name parts of the path.

| preRequestScript, postResponseScript | Scripts; they need --allow-scripts.

| timeoutMs | This request's own time limit, in ms.

### Each check in "assertions"

|

| Field | What it is

| pattern | Part of the request addresses it applies to, like "/users".

| type | status, latency, field, header, xpath, schema or same.

| path | The field (like data.items[0].id), the header name or the XPath.

| op | = != < <= > >= exists notexists contains notcontains matches

| value | What to compare with.

| enabled | false: switched off (counted once in the summary).

### "loadTest"

|

| Field | What it is

| vus, durationSec, rampUpSec, iterations | Virtual users, how long, the ramp-up, and runs per user.

| stages | [{ "duration": "30s", "targetVus": 10 }, ...] in place of vus and durationSec.

| arrivalRate | { "ratePerSec": 50, "maxVus": 100 }: a fixed rate (the open model).

| thresholds | p95, p99, maxLatencyMs, errorRatePct, droppedIterationsPct: the run fails when one is passed. With none, loadtest always exits 0.

| requests, data, dataFile | The load test's own steps and rows (otherwise the top-level ones).

| healthCheck | { "path": "/health", "intervalSec": 5 }: checked while the test runs.

## Flags several commands share

|

| Flag | What it does

| --var name=value | Sets {{name}} for this run; give the flag again for more. Commands: assert, diff, loadtest and run.

| --allow-env NAME | Lets the config read these environment variables (above). Commands: assert, diff, loadtest, run and mcp.

| --allow-scripts | Runs the pre-request and post-response scripts a config or folder holds; without it, one with scripts is refused. A script runs in a worker thread with its Node powers removed, but that is not a security sandbox: use it only for files you trust. Commands: assert, diff, run and mcp.

| --reporter junit | Writes a JUnit XML report to the file --out names, for your CI's test view. assert and run also write json and html: --reporter junit,json,html. Commands: assert, diff, run and conform.

| --baseline <file>, --update-baseline | Fails only on findings that are not in the file; --update-baseline writes this run's findings to it instead. Commit it: it holds codes and places only, no values or secrets. Commands: assert, run, conform and probe.

| --http2 | Sends every request over HTTP/2: h2 on an https address, h2c on an http one. A server that does not speak it is an error, never a quiet fall-back to HTTP/1.1. Commands: assert, diff, loadtest, run and probe.

| --cert <file>, --key <file> | A client certificate (mTLS). Commands: assert, diff, loadtest, run and probe.

| --ca <file> | Trusts a private certificate authority as well; give it again for more. Commands: assert, diff, loadtest, run and probe.

| --proxy <address> | Goes through an http proxy. Commands: assert, diff, loadtest, run and probe.

| --insecure | Skips certificate checks, for a staging server only. Commands: assert, diff, loadtest, run and probe.

| --location-trusted | On a redirect to another site, sends the credential headers (Authorization, Cookie, API keys) on too. Without it they stay behind and one line says so. Commands: assert, diff, loadtest and run.

| --cookie-jar <file> | Keeps cookies between requests, like a browser: read from the file, updated by each response and written back when the run ends. Values are never printed; keep the file out of git. Commands: assert and run.

| --data <file> | Runs the steps once per row of a CSV file (its first line names the columns) or a JSON list of objects, in place of the config's own rows. A missing, empty or broken file stops the run before any request. Commands: assert and run.

## Help in the terminal

The file carries the same help, so you can read it offline:

- node requestfox-ci.mjs --help: every command on one screen, and the exit codes.

- node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --help: one command and all of its flags.

- node requestfox-ci.mjs help config: the config file's fields, as in the tables above.

- node requestfox-ci.mjs explain RF-SLOW: what a finding code on a failure line means.

- node requestfox-ci.mjs mcp --help: the MCP server's flags.

- Run API checks in CI

A suite, a config file and one command.

# How to tell if a 401 comes from an expired token

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-401-expired-token.html

Record the page with RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox. A call refused with 401 or 403 whose bearer token (a JWT) had already run out is marked Token expired, and the line under it says how long before the call it expired. Open the call's Details: Bearer token (JWT) shows when the token was issued and when it expires. The fix is to sign in again or refresh the token. For your own requests, Compose can renew an OAuth 2.0 token before it runs out.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 17 November 2026.

## How do I see that a token expired?

### Record until the 401

Press Start Recording in RequestFox and use the app until a call fails, for example after the page sat open for an hour.

### Look for Token expired

Press Failed above the list. A call refused with 401 or 403 that sent an Authorization: Bearer token whose own expiry time had already passed is marked Token expired, and the line under it reads, for example, "The bearer token had expired 12 min before this call."

### Open the token's dates

Press Details on the card. Bearer token (JWT) lists its Algorithm, Issuer, Audience, Issued and Expires, with how long before or after this call it ran out. RequestFox reads only these fields from the token, and by default hides the token itself in everything it keeps.

### Find why the app did not renew it

Look at the calls just before the failed one. If no call to the sign-in server's token address went out, the app didn't try to refresh. If one did and failed, open it: its status and response tell you why.

### Send the call again with a new token

Sign in again in the app, or press Edit and send again… on the card and put a fresh token in its Authorization header. The new call shows as a card of its own, with its status.

## What if the token has not expired?

- The token is for another service. Compare its Issuer and Audience with what the API expects. A token for the staging server gets refused by production.

- No token was sent. Open Request headers: if there's no Authorization header, the app didn't add it, or it relies on a cookie the browser didn't send.

- The server says why. Open Response headers. A server that follows the bearer token standard answers 401 with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token" header when the token is expired, revoked, malformed or invalid in another way [1], often with an error_description.

- It's not a JWT. Some services hand out opaque tokens with no dates inside. RequestFox can't read when those expire, so the call is marked failed but not Token expired.

## Can RequestFox renew the token for my own requests?

Yes. Add a sign-in under Settings → Sign-in, cookies & connections → OAuth 2.0 & secrets vault and press Get token. In Compose, pick Bearer token and write {{oauth:My API}} in Token, with your sign-in's name. Before each send, a token about to run out (within 60 seconds) is renewed: with its refresh token, or, for Client Credentials, by asking again. Without either, Compose says "This sign-in's token has expired. Press Get token in Settings again." Tokens are kept encrypted on this device.

## Sources

- RFC 6750, "The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework: Bearer Token Usage", section 3.1. Checked 17 November 2026. rfc-editor.org

Something here out of date? Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we'll fix it.

# How to run your API checks in CI

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-api-checks-in-ci.html

Build a suite of saved requests in RequestFox, choose ··· → Export as CI config, then Download the CLI. Commit both files and run node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --config requestfox.config.json in your pipeline: it sends every request for real, checks every rule, and exits non-zero on a failure.

Needs Node 18 or newer. For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

Export as CI config, then Download the CLI.

## Steps

### Make a suite

Open Test suites from the top bar's ··· menu, name a suite and add saved requests as steps, in order. Add pass/fail checks on status, time, fields, headers or a JSON Schema.

### Export it as a CI config

On the suite's card choose ··· → Export as CI config. You get requestfox.config.json: the steps, what each one extracts, saved auth and the checks that apply.

### Download the CLI

Press Download the CLI in the same dialog. You get requestfox-ci.mjs: one file, no dependencies, shipped inside the extension.

### Commit both files

Put them next to each other in your repository.

### Run it in the pipeline

Add a step that runs node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --config requestfox.config.json --reporter junit --out results.xml and publish results.xml with your CI's JUnit report.

node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --config requestfox.config.json --reporter junit --out results.xml

## Secrets stay out of the file

A secret-looking value typed into a body, a query or a header is written as {{env:NAME}}, and the dialog lists the names. Set them as CI secrets; the run stops before any request when one is missing.

The command must also name each variable the config may read, so a changed config cannot read the job's other secrets: add --allow-env NAME (names separated by commas, or the flag again; * allows all), or set REQUESTFOX_ALLOW_ENV=NAME,NAME. The command the export dialog shows already carries the names it wrote. Without it the run stops before any request with exit code 2 and one sentence: "This config reads the environment variable NAME. Add --allow-env NAME to the command to allow it."

node requestfox-ci.mjs assert --config requestfox.config.json --allow-env API_TOKEN --reporter junit --out results.xml

In the log and the JUnit file, values of fields and headers that look like secrets are shown as "hidden". A step with no check fails when the response is 4xx or 5xx.

## More commands

- diff --save-baseline, then diff: fail when a response's shape changed since the baseline.

- conform --spec openapi.yaml --session session.json: check a recorded session against your spec. How.

- loadtest --vus 20 --duration 30s: a local load test from the same config.

- probe --spec openapi.yaml --base http://localhost:3000: tests made from your spec. Each case breaks one rule (a wrong type, a missing field, a value out of range) and your API must refuse it with a 4xx; calls that need sign-in are also sent without it. Local APIs only unless you allow otherwise; reads only unless you allow otherwise.

- mock --spec openapi.yaml: a mock API on 127.0.0.1 from your spec; --dynamic varies its responses, and --seed 42 repeats them.

- --http2 on assert, diff, loadtest, run and probe: every request goes over HTTP/2, and a server that does not speak it is an error (HTTP/3 is out of scope).

- --baseline known.json on assert, run, conform and probe: fail only on findings that are not in the file; --update-baseline writes it. explain RF-SLOW says why a finding code is flagged and what to do.

- docs --workspace folder --out docs.html: your saved requests as one API docs page, with no request sent.

Every command, flag and config field is on the command line page; in a terminal, node requestfox-ci.mjs <command> --help prints one command's flags.

## If you run Postman collections in Newman today

Newman is Postman's command-line collection runner: newman run my-collection.json -e my-environment.json [1]. Postman's own documentation now recommends the Postman CLI instead, and says Newman only supports the v2.1 collection format [2]. RequestFox's command-line tool is a different tool, not a drop-in: it does not read Postman collection files. To move a collection across:

- Import the collection (v2.0 or v2.1) in Compose with Import → Import a collection…

- Read the import summary. A Postman test made only of status, response-time, header or JSON-field assertions became checks on its request, and a value a script saved from the response into a variable became a chaining row. Any other script is named in the summary, and RequestFox does not run Postman's pm.* code.

- Put the requests in a suite, export it as a CI config and run assert as above.

Anything a Postman script did beyond that has no equivalent, so check the summary before you switch a pipeline over.

## Sources

- Postman Learning Center, "Newman CLI Overview". Checked 4 November 2026. learning.postman.com

- Postman Learning Center, "Migrate scripts from Newman to the Postman CLI". Checked 4 November 2026. learning.postman.com

Something here out of date? Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we will fix it.

## Next

- Check against OpenAPI

Live calls versus your spec, with coverage.

- For QA testers

From a manual run to a repeatable check.

# API testing in Firefox: what is built in and which extensions help

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-api-testing-firefox.html

Firefox can already test an API call with no add-on: in the Network Monitor, choose Edit and Resend on a request, change its method, address, headers or body, and send it again. For more than that, add a Firefox extension. RESTer and RESTED are REST clients: you write each request by hand. RequestFox is a browser extension that records the calls your web app makes and flags the ones that went wrong.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about Firefox and other add-ons are from their own pages, checked 4 November 2026; sources below.

## What can Firefox do on its own?

Firefox's Network Monitor lists the requests a page makes, and a request you pick can be sent again without any add-on [1][2]:

- Resend sends the request again as it was [1][2].

- Edit and Resend opens an editor where you change the method, address, headers or body, then press Send [1].

- Copy offers the request as a cURL command or as a fetch() call [2].

- Save All As HAR writes the listed requests to a HAR file [2].

- Block URL blocks the chosen address for later requests [2].

It's the quickest way to try one call you can already see. It works one request at a time, though, and deciding which calls went wrong is up to you. The extensions below add more.

## Which Firefox extensions test APIs?

These four are REST clients: you write a request and send it. The words in quotes are each listing's own summary, and the dates are the last update shown on Firefox Add-ons. They're listed in no order of merit.

|

| Extension | What its listing says | Last updated

| RESTer | "A REST client for almost any web service." Sends requests with any method, address, body and headers; saves them in collections; keeps a history of requests and responses; Basic and OAuth 2 authorization [3] | August 2026

| RESTED | "A REST client for the rest of us." The common HTTP methods, headers, saved requests and collections, URL templates, Basic auth, and import from HAR or Postman collections [4] | December 2021

| Apier | "Fast API client for HTTP, GraphQL, SOAP, WebSocket, and Socket.IO." [5] | July 2026

| API Request Tester | "Test and debug API requests directly from your browser." [6] | June 2024

A client is the right tool when you already know which request to send. RequestFox starts from the other end: it watches what your web app actually sends, so there's nothing to retype.

## How do I record the API calls a page makes in Firefox?

- Add RequestFox from Firefox Add-ons. There's no account to make.

- Open the site you want to test. Open RequestFox's sidebar and press Start Recording (or press Alt Shift S; Option Shift S on a Mac). The first time, Firefox asks you to allow access to the site.

- Use the page. Every fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket frame and server-sent event is listed as it starts, tied to the click or form submit that caused it.

- Read the flags. A call that failed, was slow, fired twice or hid an error inside a 200 OK is marked, and its card says why in plain words.

- Press Replay to send a call again, or choose Edit and send again… in its ··· menu to change it first. While recording, the call goes through the page, with its cookies.

The full steps, with the search box and what to do when nothing shows up, are in How to record API calls. Sessions stay in History, and you can export them as a HAR file, a Postman collection or an HTML report.

## What does RequestFox not do in Firefox?

- Scripts that run before a request or after a response, and rewriting a request or response with a script, work in Chrome only: Firefox does not let extensions run code typed at runtime. Chaining values from one request to the next works in both.

- Firefox has no debugger API for extensions, so there is no slow-down for the whole tab. Use a mock rule's Slow or Throttle mode for one endpoint instead.

- Clicking a RequestFox notification opens the sidebar in the window you're looking at, which may not be the window being recorded.

- It sees what a browser tab sends. Mobile and desktop apps need a proxy tool such as HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman or Charles, and there is no team workspace or cloud sync: share work as files.

Apart from these, recording, flags, mocks, checks and exports work the same in Firefox as in Chrome. The feature list says which feature is Chrome only.

## Which one should I use?

- To try one call you can already see: Edit and Resend in the Network Monitor. Nothing to install.

- To write requests by hand and keep them: a REST client such as RESTer or RESTED.

- To test your own web app as you click through it, with the broken calls found for you: RequestFox.

They fit together. Record in RequestFox, and use the built-in tools for a quick look at one request.

## Sources

- Firefox Source Docs, "Network request details". Checked 4 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

- Firefox Source Docs, "Network request list". Checked 4 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

- Firefox Add-ons, RESTer. Checked 4 November 2026. addons.mozilla.org

- Firefox Add-ons, RESTED. Checked 4 November 2026. addons.mozilla.org

- Firefox Add-ons, Apier. Checked 4 November 2026. addons.mozilla.org

- Firefox Add-ons, API Request Tester. Checked 4 November 2026. addons.mozilla.org

Something here out of date? Add-ons change. Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we'll fix it.

Start, use the site, read the flags, keep the evidence.

- Replay and edit a request

Send a recorded call again, as it was or changed.

The judging and the history, or the raw live view.

Return your own response, or make a call fail.

Add to Firefox, free

# How to send an API bug report with the evidence

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-bug-report-evidence.html

Record the bug with RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, open the call that failed and choose Copy bug report from its More menu. You get one text to paste into the ticket: the request and its status, the clicks that led to it, the console lines around it, the headers and bodies, and a cURL command that repeats it, with tokens and passwords hidden. For the whole session, Export an HTML report (screenshots included) or a HAR.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 17 November 2026.

## How do I report one failed call?

### Turn on screenshots, if you want one

In Settings → Privacy & evidence, tick Take a screenshot when a call is flagged. A flagged call then keeps a picture of the page as it was.

### Record the bug

Press Start Recording and do what goes wrong, step by step, as a user would.

### Find the call

Press Failed above the list, or search for the address. The card says what is wrong with the call, such as its status or Token expired.

### Copy the bug report

On the card, press More → Copy bug report, and paste it into the ticket or the chat.

### Check what it hid

Read it before you send it. When it hid a token, a cookie or a password, it ends with "Secrets were hidden in this copy." The developer can still repeat the call with their own sign-in.

## What does the bug report hold?

- The method and address, the page it came from, the status and how long it took.

- Its flags in capitals, such as ERROR, SLOW, TOKEN EXPIRED or GRAPHQL ERROR, and the error inside the body when there is one.

- The line of code that made the call and the click that set it off, when RequestFox saw them.

- "Steps before this call:", the steps that led up to it, and "Console around it:", the page's console errors and warnings from that moment when you record them.

- The request and response headers and bodies; a body cut short says so.

- A cURL command that sends the call again, with notes on what to fill in first.

The report is built the way Export with secrets hidden writes a file, whatever Hide passwords, tokens and card numbers in what is recorded is set to, so a token in the address or a password in a login body does not go into a ticket.

## Can I open an issue straight from the call?

Yes, in GitHub or Linear. Under Settings → Issue tracker, fill in GitHub repo (owner/repo) or Linear workspace slug. A call's More menu then offers Open GitHub issue or Open Linear issue: it opens a new issue in your browser with the title (method, path and status, never the query) and the report filled in, for you to read and submit. Nothing is sent until you press it. A long report is shortened to fit the address, and says so.

## How do I send the whole session?

Press Export at the bottom of the panel. HTML report is one file anyone can open in a browser, with each call, its flags and its screenshot; HAR opens in DevTools and other tools. With a filter on, the menu also offers to export only the calls shown. If the session still holds a token, a cookie or a password as it was sent, Export asks first: Export with secrets hidden, or Export as it is.

Exporting a HAR from Chrome's DevTools instead? Its "Export HAR (sanitized)" leaves out the Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization headers; the export with sensitive data needs a setting turned on first [1]. Tokens in an address or a body are in both.

## Sources

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 17 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

# How to change or add a request header on a site

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-change-request-headers.html

Open Header & URL rules in RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, choose Set a request header, type the part of the address it is for, the header's name and its value, and press Add rule. The rule changes the API calls of the tabs RequestFox records, while it records. To keep a header on with nothing recording, put the rule in a rule set for the sites you name and switch the set on. The same place removes a header, sets or removes a response header, and rewrites part of a URL.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 15 November 2026.

## How do I add a header to a site's requests?

### Open Header & URL rules

In RequestFox, open Settings → Mocks & rules → Header & URL rules.

### Choose what the rule does

Set a request header adds a header or replaces its value. The same list has Remove a request header, Set a response header, Remove a response header and Rewrite part of the URL.

### Say which calls it is for

In URL contains, type part of the address, such as /api/. A rule applies on the sites you record; start it with * for every site, or begin with a site's name, such as api.example.com/v1/, for that site.

### Name the header and press Add rule

Fill in the Header name, such as X-Debug, and its Value, then press Add rule. Each rule has its own switch, so you can turn one off without deleting it.

### Record, and the header goes with every matching call

Press Start Recording and use the site. The rules in this list change the API calls (fetch and XHR) of the tabs RequestFox records, while it records, and only then.

## How do I keep a header on all the time?

Use a rule set. Under Keep some rules on without recording, press New set, give it a name, the sites it is for (such as api.example.com, localhost) and its rules, one per line: header|X-Flag|beta sets a request header, removeheader|Name removes one, responseheader|Name|Value and removeresponseheader|Name do the same to the response, and rewrite|find|replace changes the address. Then switch it to Keep on.

The browser asks once to let RequestFox change requests on those sites. From then on the set changes page loads and API calls on those sites in every tab, recording or not, until you switch it off, and a chip under the top bar says which sets are on. A set is only ever on for the sites you name. Export saves your sets to one JSON file to share, and Import reads it back.

## Can I bring my ModHeader profiles?

Yes. Import under Keep some rules on without recording reads a profile file exported from ModHeader as well as RequestFox's own export. The imported sets start switched off: check their sites, then turn them on. A value that looks like a secret, such as a token, is left out of an export; after an import, those rules stay off until you fill the value in.

## What if the header does not show up?

- Nothing is recording. The Header & URL rules list works while RequestFox records. To keep a header on without that, use a rule set.

- The call is a page load, an image, a script or a stylesheet. The Header & URL rules list changes API calls (fetch and XHR) in the tabs you record. A rule set changes page loads too. Neither changes images, scripts or styles.

- The address does not match. A rule with no site in it applies on the sites you record. Start it with *, or begin it with the site's name.

- The browser refused the rule. RequestFox says so under the list and names the reason; the other rules stay on.

- A set says Needs site access. Switch it on again and allow RequestFox on that site when the browser asks.

## Can DevTools change a header?

Chrome's DevTools can override a response header locally, with DevTools open, through local overrides [1]. For a request header, or for a rule that stays on for a site in every tab, use a rule in RequestFox.

## Sources

- Chrome for Developers, "Override web content and HTTP response headers locally". Checked 15 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

# How to copy a request as cURL, and convert a cURL command to code

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-copy-as-curl-and-convert.html

In Chrome or Firefox, right-click a request in the Network panel and choose Copy, then Copy as cURL [1][2]. To turn that command into Python, JavaScript, Go or another language, paste it into RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox: in Compose open Import and press Paste a curl command…, then use More, Copy as code…, and pick the language. RequestFox copies any request as code in 15 languages, and it keeps real tokens out of what it copies unless you ask.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about browsers are from their own documentation, checked 20 November 2026; sources below.

One request as Python code, with Copy.

## How do I copy a request as cURL in Chrome, Edge or Firefox?

- Chrome: in the DevTools Network panel, right-click the request under Name, hover over Copy and choose Copy as cURL. Copy as fetch is next to it [1].

- Firefox: in the Network Monitor, right-click the request and choose Copy, then Copy as cURL [2].

The command holds the request's headers, which can include cookies and tokens. Keep it private until you have checked it.

## How do I convert a cURL command to Python, fetch or Go?

### Paste the command

In RequestFox press Compose, open Import and press Paste a curl command…. Paste it into the box and confirm. The status line says Filled from the cURL command. The method, address, headers and body are now in the request. Form fields that sent a file are left out, and a note says which.

### Check it, and send it if you like

Press Send to see the response. It also works as a way to check that the command still does what you meant.

### Open Copy as code

Open the request's More menu and choose Copy as code….

### Pick the language and copy

Choose a Language and press Copy. The choices are cURL for bash and for Windows cmd, PowerShell, JavaScript (fetch), Node.js (fetch), Python (requests), HTTPie, Go (net/http), Java (HttpClient), C# (HttpClient), PHP (cURL), Ruby (Net::HTTP), Swift (URLSession), Kotlin (OkHttp) and Rust (reqwest).

If the box says it does not look like a curl command, the text has to start with curl.

## Can I copy a call I recorded as cURL or code?

Yes, with no browser menu to find. Open the call's card, then More: Copy as cURL copies it as a command, and Copy as code… opens the same language list. How to record API calls shows how a call gets there.

## Will a token end up in the code I copy?

Not by default. While Hide passwords, tokens and card numbers in what is recorded is on in Settings, hidden values show as ***REDACTED*** in the copied code, and a note tells you to put the real ones in. A secret that came from an environment is kept as a variable, with a note to set its value before you run the code. If you need the real values, Use the real URL and headers shows them, with a warning that the code holds live secrets and should not be shared.

# How to find why an API call is blocked by CORS

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-cors-blocked-call.html

Record the page with RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, and open the failed call: its card says CORS where the status goes, and the line under it names the rule that blocked it, such as "the response has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header" or "the call was sent with cookies, so the server must name this page's origin, not *". Press Replay from the extension to see what the server really sent back. The fix is on the server: it must allow the page's origin.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 17 November 2026.

## How do I see why the browser blocked a call?

### Record the page

Open the page in a tab, press Start Recording in RequestFox and do what fails, such as signing in or saving a form.

### Find the call marked CORS

Press Failed above the list. A call the browser blocked for CORS shows CORS where its status would be. When the browser asked permission first, that check shows as a card of its own, marked preflight.

### Read the reason under it

The line under the call names the rule that failed, for example Blocked by CORS: the response has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. The next section says what each one means.

### See what the server sent

Press Replay from the extension on the card. RequestFox sends the call itself, where the browser's CORS rule does not apply and without the page's cookies, so you can read the status, the headers and the body the page was not allowed to see.

### Fix it on the server

The server must send Access-Control-Allow-Origin with the page's origin, and for a call with cookies also Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Record again: the call should pass, and leave the Failed list.

## What does each CORS reason mean?

RequestFox checks in the order the browser does, from the page's origin, the call's own headers and what the server sent, and names the first rule that failed:

- The permission check (preflight) got no response, or a status that is not 2xx. Before a call with a custom header, a JSON body or a method other than GET, HEAD or POST, the browser first sends an OPTIONS request [1]. The server must answer it with a 2xx.

- The preflight does not allow this page's origin, the method or a header. Its Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods or Access-Control-Allow-Headers must include them. A * in Allow-Headers never covers Authorization: name it.

- The response has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header. The call reached the server, but the server did not say this origin may read the response.

- The response allows another origin. The header names a different site, often the production address on a test site.

- The call was sent with cookies, so the server must name this page's origin, not *. With credentials, the browser refuses the wildcard [1].

- The call was sent with cookies, but the response has no Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

## Can I keep testing until the server is fixed?

Yes, two ways. In Compose, a request the page could not send says so, and Send from the extension instead sends it without the CORS block (and without the page's cookies). Or add a Set a response header rule under Header & URL rules that gives the page an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header while the backend's CORS isn't ready. Remove the rule when the server is fixed: it changes what the page receives, not the server.

## What if the card only says "Most likely blocked by CORS"?

The browser does not tell extensions why a call failed. RequestFox marks a call to another origin that failed with the browser's generic error as most likely CORS, and names the rule only when the headers show it. If no reason shows, an ad blocker or privacy extension may have blocked the call instead: reload with your other extensions switched off. Optionally, Allow the security probe on a call (OPTIONS) in Settings → Privacy & evidence adds a Security probe (OPTIONS) item to a card's menu: after you confirm, it sends one real OPTIONS request and reads what the server says it allows. It is not a full browser preflight, so a real CORS error can still happen.

## Sources

- MDN Web Docs, "Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)". Checked 17 November 2026. developer.mozilla.org

Something here out of date? Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we will fix it.
