# How to find duplicate and N+1 API calls in a web app

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-duplicate-and-n-plus-one-api-calls.html

A duplicate API call is the same request sent more than once, usually by accident. An N+1 pattern is one request per item in a list, such as /items/1, /items/2, /items/3, where one batched request would do. To find them, filter the DevTools Network panel to Fetch/XHR and look for repeats. Or record with RequestFox, a browser extension that marks a repeat as Duplicate or Retry, shows a burst as One call per item, and points to the click that caused each call.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about other tools are from their own pages, checked 4 November 2026; sources below.

## Why does my page send the same API call twice?

The usual causes: two parts of the page ask for the same data, a click or a form submit is handled twice, or code sends the call again after a failure. Some repeats are on purpose, like polling or a heartbeat.

If you're building a React app, there's one more. With Strict Mode on, React runs one extra setup and cleanup cycle for every Effect in development [2], so a fetch inside an Effect can show up twice on your machine. React says these checks are development only and don't affect the production build [2]. Look at a production build before you call it a bug.

## What is an N+1 API call pattern?

It's a performance problem where an application makes many network requests to fetch one type of resource: one request for each item in a list, instead of one combined request [1]. It often shows up when a page renders a list or a grid and each item loads its own data [1].

Each call costs time, and the cost adds up with the length of the list. Fixes depend on the app, and some of this may be on purpose [1]. Common ones: fetch the data for all items in one call, for example an endpoint that takes a list of ids; load an item's data only when it comes into view; or cache the data, or share one call between the parts that ask for it [1].

## How do I find duplicate calls by hand in DevTools?

- Open the DevTools Network panel and choose the Fetch/XHR filter [3].

- Reload the page or repeat the action, and look down the list for the same address more than once.

- Look at the Waterfall, which orders requests by start time [3]. A stack of near-identical bars that start together is a burst.

- To see what sent a call, hover over its Initiator column: for a call made by JavaScript it shows the stack trace leading up to the request [3].

This works, and it costs nothing. But you count by eye, and the list is gone when you close the panel. For the failed and slow calls, see how to find failed and slow API calls in Chrome.

## How does RequestFox flag duplicate and N+1 calls?

Press Start, use the page, and look for these marks. They're the panel's own labels.

- Duplicate · after 140 ms the same call fired again within the rapid cutoff: likely a bug

- Retry · after 900 ms the same call sent again later, within the window: possibly a retry

- One call per item N+1: one call per id in a quick burst

How it decides:

- Duplicates: the same method, address and body, from the same tab, inside the time set by Count a repeat as a duplicate within (ms) (2 seconds at first). A repeat faster than Flag a repeat as a likely bug when faster than (ms) (500 ms at first) is marked Duplicate; a slower one, Retry. Both numbers are in Settings.

- N+1: five or more different ids on one endpoint inside three seconds show as One call per item under Repeated problems above the log, with the number of calls and how long the burst took. Click it to see them. A GraphQL operation or JSON-RPC method sent again and again with different variables counts too, inside one second.

- The cause: every flagged call is tied to the click or form submit that caused it, and Details → Called from lists the page code that made the call.

- Repeats you expect: on a card, ··· More → Stop flagging repeats keeps that endpoint's repeats, such as polling, from being flagged.

RequestFox marks what it sees, and you decide which repeats are bugs. It only sees what a browser tab sends. How to record API calls.

## How do I fix them, and check the fix?

Pick the fix that fits [1]: one combined call, loading on demand, or a cache that shares one call. For a repeat that only shows in development, check a production build first [2].

Then record the same flow again. Every session stays in History, so you can open the earlier one next to the new one and see whether the repeats are gone.

## Sources

- Sentry documentation, "N+1 API Calls". Checked 4 November 2026. docs.sentry.io

- React documentation, "StrictMode". Checked 4 November 2026. react.dev

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 4 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

Something here out of date? Docs change. Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we'll fix it.

# How to find failed and slow API calls in Chrome

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-find-failed-and-slow-api-calls.html

Open DevTools (Ctrl Shift J), click Network, choose Fetch/XHR, tick Preserve log, then sort by Status to see the failed calls and by Time to see the slow ones. You don't need to install anything. But a call that fails inside a 200 OK still looks fine there. RequestFox, a browser extension, counts the failed and slow calls while you use the site, and marks the ones that fail inside a 200.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about Chrome are from its own documentation, checked 4 November 2026; sources below.

## How do I find failed and slow requests in Chrome DevTools?

### Open the Network panel

Press Ctrl Shift J (Cmd Option J on a Mac), then click the Network tab [2]. DevTools only records requests while it's open [2], so open it before you do the thing that breaks.

### Show only API calls

Click the Fetch/XHR button among the type filters [1]. Tick Preserve log, and DevTools keeps the requests across page loads until you untick it [1]. Without it, a page that reloads after the error clears the list.

### Find the failed calls

Click the Status column header to sort by it [1]. The column shows the HTTP code, for example 200 or 404. A request that failed before it got a response shows (failed) followed by the error message, and a CORS failure shows CORS error [1]. To see only one code, type status-code:500 in the Filter box [1]. To see everything except what the filter matches, tick Invert next to the box [1].

### Find the slow calls

Click the Time column header to sort by it [1]. Time is the total duration, from the start of the request to the last byte of the response [1]. To sort the Waterfall by a different timing, right-click the table header, hover Waterfall and pick Start Time, Response Time, End Time, Total Duration or Latency [1]. To find big responses, filter with larger-than:1000; larger-than:1k works too [1].

### See where the time went

Click a slow request and open its Timing tab [1]. The phases include Queueing, Stalled, DNS Lookup, Initial connection, Request sent, Waiting (TTFB) and Content Download. Waiting (TTFB) is the time the browser waits for the first byte of the response. It includes one round trip of latency and the time the server took to prepare the response [1].

### Search every response

Press Ctrl F (Cmd F on a Mac) in the Network panel. The Search tab opens and looks through request headers, payloads and responses. Click a result and the matching request is highlighted [1]. It's a quick way to find which call returned an error message you saw on screen.

## What can DevTools not show me?

- One call at a time. You sort and read a long table, then open each suspect to read its response. The table doesn't count how many calls failed or were slow.

- Errors inside a 200. The Status column shows the HTTP code. An API that sends a 200 and puts the failure in the body, as GraphQL does, looks fine in the list. You find it by opening the response, or by searching for the error text. GraphQL errors in a 200 OK.

- It only keeps what you watched. DevTools records while it's open, and you have to tick Preserve log before the page moves on.

- The cause is a separate hunt. For a request started by a script, the Initiator column links to the line in the source file [1], and you follow it by hand for each call.

## How does RequestFox find them for me?

- Press Start Recording, then use the site. Every API call shows up in the panel, with the failed, slow and repeated ones marked. How to record API calls.

- Read the counts. Above the calls are buttons for Duplicate, Failed, Slow and JS errors. Click one to see only those calls, and click it again to see them all.

- Know what counts as Failed. A call is Failed when its status is 400 or higher, when it never got a status (connection refused, a CORS block, aborted), or when the response says it failed inside a 200 OK: a GraphQL errors list, a JSON-RPC error, a SOAP fault, an error event inside an event stream, or a gRPC status other than OK. Those calls carry their own mark, such as GraphQL error, so you can tell them from a plain 500.

- Know what counts as Slow. A call is Slow when it takes longer than your slow limit. The limit starts at 3 seconds, and you change it in Settings under When to flag a call, in the box Flag a call as slow after (ms). The Slow mark on a card says the limit in its tooltip.

- Check Repeated problems. When endpoints keep failing or being slow, they are listed above the log under Repeated problems, with how many times each failed or was slow, so one bad endpoint doesn't get lost among hundreds of cards.

- Open a call to see why. Its Timing section shows where the time went: queued, DNS lookup, connect, waiting for the server, download. For a call to another site, the browser hides the breakdown unless that server allows it, and the card says so. Called from lists the page code that made the call.

- Send it again. Press Replay on a card to resend that exact request and see whether it still fails. For a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE it asks first, because a repeat can change real data. Replay and edit a request.

RequestFox marks what it sees, and you decide what's a bug. A call that your own mock or fault rule changed is marked Mocked or Simulated, so a test you set up isn't mistaken for a real failure.

Watch it in 37 seconds on YouTube

## Which should I use when?

|

| You want to | Use

| Look at one call right now, with nothing installed | DevTools. It's built in, exact, and shows every phase of a request.

| Filter by one status code or one size | DevTools. The Filter box does that in one line.

| Know how many calls failed or were slow in a whole session | RequestFox. The counts sit above the log, and you can click them.

| Catch a failure the status code hides | RequestFox marks GraphQL, JSON-RPC, SOAP and stream errors in a 200. In DevTools you read the body.

| Find the code that made a call, or send it again | RequestFox: Called from and Replay on the card.

| Keep the evidence after you close the tab | RequestFox keeps each session in History. Send a bug report with the evidence.

They work together: DevTools for the exact one-call view, RequestFox for the whole session. RequestFox vs DevTools Network.

# GraphQL returns 200 OK with errors: how to spot and catch it

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-graphql-errors-in-200.html

A GraphQL call can come back 200 OK and still have failed. Read the response body. If it has a top-level errors list, something went wrong, in all of the call or just part of it, whatever the HTTP status says. RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, marks such a call "GraphQL error", and its command-line tool can fail a CI run on it.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about GraphQL and other tools are from their own pages, checked 4 November 2026; sources below.

## Why does a failed GraphQL call come back 200 OK?

A GraphQL response is a JSON object. Its data entry holds the result and its errors entry holds what went wrong [1]. A field that fails is replaced with null while the rest of the result still arrives, so one response can hold both [1].

HTTP has no status code for "partly worked". The GraphQL project's guidance is that a response with a data entry that is not null gets a 2xx status, even when it also has errors [2]. The GraphQL-over-HTTP draft says the same, and calls a 4xx or 5xx "not appropriate" for a partial result [3].

When a request fails before it runs, because of a syntax or validation error, the response has no data entry. Servers usually answer 400 then, but the GraphQL project notes that some older servers answer 2xx when the response type is application/json [2]. Some APIs use 200 for every error in the application itself: monday.com's API documentation says it answers 200 OK for those and keeps other statuses for problems in transport [4].

So the status isn't enough. Read the body.

## What does a GraphQL error look like?

For example, the user was found but one of its fields failed:

{
"data": { "user": { "name": "Ada", "photo": null } },
"errors": [
{ "message": "Photo unavailable.", "path": ["user", "photo"] }
]
}

Every error has a message. It may also have locations (the line and column in your query), a path (which field failed) and extensions (extra detail the API adds) [1]. Three shapes are common:

- Partial result: most fields arrived, the failed ones are null, and path says which. A page built from this may look half empty.

- No result: data is null, because an error stopped the whole result [1].

- No data entry at all: the request never ran, for example a syntax error in the query [1].

## How do I spot it in the browser by hand?

- Open the DevTools Network panel and choose the Fetch/XHR filter [5].

- Click the GraphQL call. A GraphQL API is typically one address ending in /graphql [2], so the address doesn't tell you which operation it was. Read the request to find out.

- Open its response and look for errors. The status column will still say 200.

This works for one call you're already looking at. It won't warn you about the one you didn't open. For failed and slow calls in general, see how to find failed and slow API calls in Chrome.

## How does RequestFox catch it for me?

### Record the calls

Press Start Recording in RequestFox and use your app. How to record API calls.

### Look for the GraphQL error mark

A call whose response holds an errors list is marked "GraphQL error", and it's listed among the session's findings in the Session overview. A 4xx or 5xx response is already marked Failed by its status.

### Open the call

The card shows the first error's message and, when there are more, how many. Open it to read the whole response.

### Press "Why is this flagged?"

The finding code is RF-GQL-ERROR. The panel explains it offline, and requestfox-ci explain RF-GQL-ERROR says the same in a terminal.

What RequestFox looks for, so you know what it will and won't flag:

- The response is JSON with an errors list in which every error is an object with a text message.

- The call looks like GraphQL: its address contains "graphql", or a ?query= holds an operation, or the request body has a query that reads like a GraphQL document or a persisted-query id. A REST API that lists "errors" for its own reasons isn't marked as GraphQL.

- A batch (a list of responses) counts if any one of them failed.

- A response cut off at the body size limit isn't read.

This rule won't catch a server that reports failure some other way, such as a field named error or a status inside data. For that, add a check on the field to the endpoint: checks can test fields, status, time and headers.

## How do I make a CI run fail on it?

The command-line tool, requestfox-ci, makes the same check. In assert, a step whose response carries GraphQL errors fails with "no GraphQL error". For a suite that tests error paths on purpose, put "bodyErrors": false in its config to switch the check off. How to run API checks in CI.

## How do I test how my app handles a GraphQL error?

Make the API return one. Record the real call, open its card and press Mock, keep the status at 200 and change the body to a response with an errors list, then press Mock it. Reload the page: it gets your response, and the card says Mocked so nobody files it as a bug. How to mock an API response.

## Sources

- GraphQL specification, October 2021, section 7 "Response". Checked 4 November 2026. spec.graphql.org

- GraphQL.org, "Serving over HTTP", Status Codes. Checked 4 November 2026. graphql.org

- GraphQL over HTTP, current working draft, section 5.4 "Status Codes". A draft, not a final standard. Checked 4 November 2026. http-spec.graphql.org

- monday.com developer documentation, "Error handling". Checked 4 November 2026. developer.monday.com

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 4 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

# How to open and read a HAR file in your browser, offline

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-har-file-viewer.html

To read a HAR file without uploading it anywhere, open it in RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox. In History, press Open file…, pick the .har file, then open it from the list. Every call is listed with its status, timing, headers and bodies, and the failed, slow, repeated and hidden-error calls are flagged. The file is read on your computer, and nothing is sent to us.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about browsers are from their own documentation, checked 20 November 2026; sources below.

A file you open lands in History, beside your own recordings.

## Where do I get a HAR file?

- Chrome: in the DevTools Network panel, press Export HAR (sanitized)… in the bar at the top of the panel [1].

- Firefox: in the Network Monitor, right-click a request and choose Save All As HAR [2].

- RequestFox: a session you recorded exports as HAR from the Export menu, and from History (its More menu).

A file someone sent you for a bug report works the same way.

## How do I open a HAR file?

### Open History

In RequestFox, press History in the top bar.

### Press Open file…

Pick the .har file. Files up to 256 MB open. A dialog titled File opened says how many requests were loaded into History, and what was hidden (see below).

### Open it from the list

The file shows up as a session named after it, starting with "Imported:". Press its name to open it in the log, read-only. Your own recordings stay as they were.

### Find the call you need

Type in Search calls: a word matches the address, the method or the status, and filters such as status:>=400 or latency:>1000 narrow it down. Open a card to read its headers, body and timing.

### Take it further

Press Report on the session for an HTML report, or open its More menu for CSV, JSON, a Postman collection and more. Compare to current sets it against what you're recording now.

A RequestFox session file (.requestfox or .json) opens the same way, with its flags and console log.

## What does RequestFox flag in a HAR file?

The same things it flags in a live recording, read from the file:

- calls that failed: a status of 400 or more, or a network error;

- slow calls, over the limit set in Settings (Flag a call as slow after (ms));

- repeated calls: the same request again within a short time;

- errors inside a 200 OK, in GraphQL, JSON-RPC and SOAP responses;

- streams that sent an error event.

Browsers' own preflight checks (the OPTIONS call before a cross-origin call) aren't counted as slow or repeated.

## Are the tokens in the file shown?

Not by default. While Hide passwords, tokens and card numbers in what is recorded is on in Settings, tokens, passwords and cookies in an opened file are hidden as it opens, and the File opened dialog lists what was hidden, by kind. Turn that setting off and the file opens as it is. To pass the file on without them, see how to clean a HAR file before you share it.

## What does it not show?

- A HAR holds what the Network panel held. It has no console log, so none is shown. A RequestFox session file does.

- The Cookie header, Host, Connection, Content-Length and HTTP/2 pseudo-headers are left out when a HAR is read.

- A file with no requests in it, or that isn't a HAR or a session file, is refused with a message saying so.

## Sources

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 20 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Firefox Source Docs, "Network request list". Checked 20 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

Something here out of date? Tools change. Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we'll fix it.

# HAR to Postman: three ways to get your browser's API calls into Postman

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-har-to-postman.html

Postman's import page lists Postman files, API specs, cURL commands and other API clients. A HAR file is not on the list [1]. Three routes end in something Postman does list: copy a call as cURL in DevTools and import it; read the HAR in RequestFox, a browser extension, and export a Postman collection; or skip the HAR, record the calls in RequestFox and export the collection. A HAR can hold cookies and tokens, so read it before you share it.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about Postman and browsers are from their own documentation, checked 4 November 2026; sources below.

## How do I save a HAR file from my browser?

- Chrome: in the DevTools Network panel, right-click a request and choose Copy → Save all as HAR (sanitized), or press Export HAR (sanitized)… in the bar at the top of the panel [2].

- Firefox: in the Network Monitor, right-click a request and choose Save All As HAR [3].

Both write the requests listed in the panel at that moment. Reload the page with the panel open first, so the file holds the calls you want.

## Does Postman import a HAR file?

Postman's import page, checked on the date above, lists what it reads: files exported from Postman (collections, environments, globals and data dumps), API definitions such as OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, protobuf and GraphQL, cURL commands, Git repositories, and data from SoapUI, Hoppscotch, Insomnia and Thunder Client [1]. It does not name HAR.

This guide does not depend on it. Each way below ends in a collection or a cURL command, which Postman lists.

## Way 1: how do I turn one call into Postman with cURL?

- In the Network panel, right-click the request and choose Copy → Copy as cURL [2][3].

- In Postman, choose Use resources or import, open the Import tab, paste the command, and choose Import Into Collection to keep it, or Import without saving to just open it [1]. You can also paste a cURL command straight into a request's address box [1].

Good for one call or a few. For a whole flow, it is slow.

## Way 2: how do I turn a HAR file into a Postman collection with RequestFox?

- In RequestFox, open Compose, open Import and press Import a collection…. Pick the .har file. RequestFox saves the requests in it as a collection you can send, copy as code or edit.

- Open the collection's More menu and choose Export…, then Postman. If the collection holds a real token, password, API key or cookie, RequestFox asks first. The default button, Export without credentials, writes each one as a {{variable}} for you to fill in.

- In Postman, choose Use resources or import, open the Import tab and pick the file [1]. The file is a Postman Collection v2.1.

Reading a HAR, RequestFox leaves out the Cookie header, Host, Connection, Content-Length and HTTP/2 pseudo-headers. It keeps the other headers, Authorization included, so take secrets out of the HAR first or let the export remove them.

## Way 3: how do I skip the HAR and record in RequestFox?

If you can reproduce the flow, record it again. Press Start in RequestFox, use the site, press Stop, then press Export (bottom right) and choose Postman collection. Sessions you recorded earlier are in History: on a session, ··· More → Postman collection, the same words as the Export menu. No HAR file with your tokens in it is needed, and RequestFox redacts Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields by default in what you view or export. How to record API calls.

## What should I remove from a HAR file before I share it?

A HAR is a copy of what your browser sent and received. Chrome leaves Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization headers out of the file by default, and only includes them if you turn on a setting and choose the "with sensitive data" export [2]. Tokens can also sit in an address, a request body or a response, so read the file before you send it to anyone. If you use Firefox, check what its file holds.

RequestFox's Security mark flags some of these as you record, such as a token in an address.

## Sources

- Postman Docs, "Import data into Postman". Checked 4 November 2026. learning.postman.com

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 4 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Firefox Source Docs, "Network request list". Checked 4 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

Something here out of date? Tools change. Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we will fix it.

# How to import a Postman collection and run it in the browser

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-import-postman-collection.html

Export the collection from Postman as a JSON file, then in RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, open Compose → Import → Import a collection… and pick the file. RequestFox saves it under Saved collections: a file with folders becomes one folder named after the file, its folders kept, with their variables and auth. It turns the common tests (status, time, header and JSON field checks, and saved values) into checks and chaining rows, and lists every script it couldn't turn into one. Then send any request from it, or run the whole file as a suite from its folder's menu.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 17 November 2026.

## How do I move a collection from Postman?

### Export it from Postman

In Postman, open Collections, then the collection's View more actions menu → More → Export collection, and save the JSON file. Postman writes Collection Format v2.1 [1]. RequestFox reads v2.0 and v2.1.

### Import it into RequestFox

Open Compose, then Import → Import a collection…, and pick the file. A file on a web server works too: Import from URL….

### Read what it kept

The note after the import says what came along, such as "Kept its variables (4) and its auth in Collection settings." and "Made checks (6) and chaining rows (2) from its tests, each on its own request.", then what was left out and why.

### Fill in what a file can't carry

Each OAuth 2.0 sign-in in the file gets a button, “Add “My API” as a sign-in…” with its own name: press it and type the client secret, which the file doesn't hold. Pick files for form fields in Compose before you send.

### Send a request, or run them all

Pick a request and press Send. To run the whole file with its checks, open the menu of its folder (or of one collection) in the saved collections and choose Run as a suite….

## Which Postman tests come along?

The common ones become checks that need no code, so they run in Chrome, in Firefox and in the command line in CI: a test of the status, the response time, a header or a JSON field becomes a check on that request, and pm.environment.set("name", pm.response.json().path) becomes a chaining row that saves the value for the next request.

A test with anything else in it isn't run. The import lists it under "Scripts not translated", and the script stays on the request, so exporting to Postman gives it back as it was. To bring one over by hand, paste it into a RequestFox script box in Chrome: each pm. line is pointed out with its rf. twin, and one button fixes all of them.

## What do I have to set up again?

- Environments. A Postman environment is its own file [1], not part of the collection, and RequestFox doesn't read it. Make a RequestFox environment with the same variable names, or import a .env file with Import .env….

- Variables with no value here. Postman variables the collection doesn't define are sent as written, and the import lists them: give each a value or an environment variable.

- Files. A form field or a body that is a file can't come along in a collection file, and the import names those requests.

- Old files. A Postman v1 file is refused with "This is a Postman v1 file. Export it from Postman as Collection v2.1."

## Can I take it back to Postman?

Yes. A saved collection's Export… can write a Postman Collection v2.1 file, with the untranslated scripts as they came, and a folder's Export… writes the whole imported file back as one collection with its folders. It tells you what Postman can't run or read, like RequestFox's own checks and chaining rows. A recorded session also exports as a Postman collection from Export at the bottom of the panel.

## Sources

- Postman Docs, "Export data from Postman". Checked 17 November 2026. learning.postman.com

Something here out of date? Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we'll fix it.

# How to intercept and modify API calls in Chrome

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-intercept-api-calls-chrome.html

Chrome DevTools already does part of it: override a response with a local file, block a request, and resend a request you edit as a fetch() call [1][2]. A browser extension gets you there faster. In RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, record the call, press Mock on its card, change the status or body and press Mock it, and the page gets your response. To change a request, use Edit and send again… in its card's More menu. The details and limits are below.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about Chrome are from its own documentation, checked 20 November 2026; sources below.

## Can Chrome DevTools intercept and change an API call?

- Change a response: right-click the request in the Network panel and choose Override content or Override headers. DevTools saves a copy of the file in a folder you choose and serves it on reload [1].

- Resend a request: Edit and resend as fetch opens the Console with the request written as a fetch() call; change it and press Enter [2]. Since Chrome 152 the old Replay XHR item is called Resend, and it handles every fetchable request [3].

- Block a request: the Network request blocking tab in the drawer [2].

Overrides turn the browser cache off while they're on, and the changes are files you manage in a folder [1].

## How do I change a response with RequestFox?

### Record the real call

Press Start Recording and do what makes the call.

### Press Mock on its card

Open the card and press Mock. The dialog holds the status and body the server sent.

### Change it and press Mock it

Edit the status or body, then press Mock it. Reload the page: it gets your response, and the card says Mocked.

To make a call fail, slow or pause instead, add a rule under Settings: modes include Network error, Slow and a breakpoint on the request or the response. Mock an API response has every step, and Change a request header covers headers and addresses.

## How do I change a request and send it again?

Open the call's card, open its More menu and choose Edit and send again…. Change the method, address, headers or body, and send. The edited call shows up as a new card at the top of the log, and the Compare with the original link puts the two side by side. Replay and edit a request has the details.

## DevTools or an extension?

|

| | Chrome DevTools | RequestFox

| Change a response | Override content: edit a saved copy in Sources [1] | Mock on the card: edit the status and body in a dialog

| Change a request | Edit and resend as fetch, in the Console [2] | Edit and send again…, with a Compare with the original

| Where the change lives | Files in a folder you choose [1] | A rule in the extension, with a label on the call (Mocked)

| Worth knowing | The cache is off while overrides are on [1] | Only calls the page makes with fetch or XMLHttpRequest, while recording or kept on

## Which one should I use?

- A quick change to one file, with nothing to install: DevTools overrides.

- An error, an empty list or a slow response to test a screen: a RequestFox mock, labelled so nobody files it as a bug.

- A request you want to tweak and compare: Edit and send again…, or DevTools' Edit and resend as fetch.

A mock doesn't answer calls from a worker, images or scripts. It's for calls the page makes itself. RequestFox vs the DevTools Network panel has the rest.

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 20 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Chrome for Developers, "What's new in DevTools (Chrome 152)". Checked 20 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

Something here out of date? Chrome changes often. Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we'll fix it.

# How to mock an API for Playwright or Cypress tests

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-mock-api-playwright-cypress.html

The mock itself lives in your test code: Playwright answers a request with page.route and route.fulfill [1], and Cypress with cy.intercept and a static response [2]. RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, doesn't write those mocks for you. It helps around them: record the real call to get the exact response to copy into your mock, mock a call by hand in the browser while you build a screen, and export a recording as a Playwright or Cypress test that calls the real API and checks what came back.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about Playwright and Cypress are from their own documentation, checked 20 November 2026; sources below.

## How do I mock an API in Playwright or Cypress?

- Playwright: page.route() catches requests that match a URL pattern, and route.fulfill() answers them with data you supply. route.fetch() makes the real request so you can change its response first, and page.routeFromHAR() replays requests from a HAR file [1].

- Cypress: cy.intercept() can spy on requests, stub their responses, or both. A static response with a statusCode, headers and body, or a fixture, is the stub [2].

Both run inside the test, so the mock lives in your repository and runs in CI.

## Where does RequestFox help?

A mock is only as good as the response behind it. Press Start Recording, use the page, and open the call's card: Response shows the real status, headers and body to copy into route.fulfill() or a Cypress fixture. If a bug only shows on some responses, the failed and odd calls are already flagged for you. How to record API calls.

## Can I mock a call in the browser, to build or test by hand?

### Record the call

Press Start Recording and do what makes the call.

### Press Mock on the card

Open the card and press Mock. Change the status or the body to an error, an empty list or a missing field.

### Press Mock it and reload

Press Mock it and reload the page. It gets your response, and the card says Mocked.

This mock answers the page in your own browser, while RequestFox records the tab or keeps it on. It doesn't run inside a Playwright or Cypress run. Mock an API response has every step.

## How do I export a Playwright or Cypress test from a recording?

### Record the flow

Press Start Recording, use the app, press Stop.

### Choose the test code

Press Export (bottom right) and, under Functional test code, choose Playwright test or Cypress test.

### Run the file

The comment at the top of the file gives the command to run it.

The file has one test per recorded request. A Playwright test uses the request fixture and a Cypress test uses cy.request. Each test sends the request to the real API and checks the status that was recorded and the top-level shape of the response. A value that one response returns, such as an id or a token, is passed on to the requests after it. A token or other secret header isn't written into the file. It becomes a named setting read from the environment, and the top of the file says which ones to set. These tests call the API for real; they don't mock it.

## What does RequestFox not do here?

- It does not generate page.route() or cy.intercept() code.

- It doesn't mock inside your test run. Its mocks live in the extension, in your browser.

- If you keep a HAR file in your repository for Playwright to replay, clean it of tokens first.

## Sources

- Playwright, "Mock APIs". Checked 20 November 2026. playwright.dev

- Cypress, "intercept". Checked 20 November 2026. docs.cypress.io

Something here out of date? Tools change. Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we'll fix it.

# How to mock an API response without a backend

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-mock-api-response.html

RequestFox is a browser extension that can mock an API response without a backend: open a recorded call and press Mock on its card, change the status or the body if you want, then press Mock it and reload the page. From then on the page gets your response instead of the server's, for the calls it makes with fetch and XMLHttpRequest, and the call is labelled Mocked. Chrome DevTools local overrides and Mock Service Worker are two other ways, compared below.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

Press Mock on a call, change the response, press Mock it.

## Steps

### Record the real call once

Press Start Recording and do what makes the call, so RequestFox has its real status, headers and body to start from.

### Press Mock on the card

Open the call's card and press Mock, next to Replay. The dialog holds the response the server sent: its status and its body. It also works for a call that got no response at all (the backend is down). Then it starts with 200 and {}.

### Change the response, then Mock it

Change the status or the body to what you want to test: an empty list, an error, a missing field. Press Mock it. More options… opens the full rule (method, how the address is matched, content type, a GraphQL operation).

### Make the call again

Reload the page, or do the action in the page again. The page receives your response, and the card shows Mocked so nobody files it as a bug. Replay and Compose always call the real server, so use the page itself to see the mock.

Watch it in 20 seconds on YouTube

## If the mock does not answer

Open the call again. When a mock didn't answer it, the card says why, in these words:

- The card says Not mocked: its mock is switched off. Press Mock off on the card, then Turn on.

- Not mocked: the page made this call before RequestFox was ready. Reload the page again. The page's very first calls can come before RequestFox is ready, and a second reload catches them.

- Not mocked: the page itself did not make this call (a worker, a beacon or a frame RequestFox can't reach), so a mock can't answer it. Mock the call the page makes instead, if there is one.

- You pressed Replay or sent it from Compose: Not mocked: Replay and Compose always call the real server. Use the page itself.

- Nothing is recording and the mock isn't kept on: the card says Mock paused. Press Start Recording, or keep it on (below).

- The page still shows old data: reload it. A mock answers the next call, not one the page already made.

## Keep a mock on without recording

On the card press Mocked, then Keep it on without recording…, and name the site (for example localhost). The mock then answers on that site in every tab, with nothing recording, until you turn it off. A chip under the top bar says Mock set on: localhost, with the set's name.

## Mock a call that was never recorded

Settings → Mocks & rules → Mock or break an endpoint → Add rule…, with the mode Mock: type the part of the address to match, the status and the body.

## Break a call instead

Settings → Mocks & rules → Mock or break an endpoint → Add rule…. Give the part of the address to match, a method, and a mode:

- Fail: answer with an error status you pick.

- Network error: fail the way a dropped connection does.

- Slow or Throttle: add a delay, or slow the response by its size.

- Mock: return the response you write.

- Breakpoint (request) or Breakpoint (response): pause the call so you can edit it before it goes on.

- Cycle: answer differently on each call.

Calls you broke on purpose are labelled Simulated.

Rules that mock or break endpoints.

## When you are done

The call's card says Mocked: press it to edit the response, keep it on without recording, turn it off or delete the mock. After Stop it says Mock paused, and the mock waits for the next recording. While any rule is on, the recording bar says "Mocks on (n)": press it to see every rule. A mock answers only while RequestFox records the tab, unless you keep it on without recording, and only the calls the page makes with fetch or XMLHttpRequest (not a worker's calls, images or scripts).

## DevTools local overrides, Mock Service Worker or an extension?

Here are three ways to change what an API call returns in the browser, side by side. Local overrides are part of Chrome DevTools, so there's nothing to install. Mock Service Worker is a library you add to your own app. An extension such as RequestFox works on any site and starts from a call it recorded.

|

| | DevTools local overrides | Mock Service Worker | RequestFox mock rule

| Where it lives | In Chrome DevTools; changes are saved as files in a folder you choose [1] | A library in your own project's code [2] | In the extension, beside your page

| Needs the app's code | No; it can mock resources you have no access to [1] | Yes | No

| What it changes | A response's content and headers, including XHR and fetch responses [1] | The requests your app makes: it intercepts, observes and changes them [2] | The status, headers and body of a call it recorded; or it makes a call fail, slow down or pause

| Worth knowing | It turns the browser cache off while overrides are on [1] | In the browser it uses the Service Worker API; in Node.js it works differently [2] | It changes fetch and XMLHttpRequest calls the page makes, and labels them Mocked or Simulated

RequestFox vs the DevTools Network panel.

## Sources

- Chrome for Developers, "Override web content and HTTP response headers locally". Checked 4 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Mock Service Worker, "Introduction". Checked 4 November 2026. mswjs.io

# Check API calls against an OpenAPI spec

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-openapi-contract-check.html

RequestFox is a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox that checks the API calls your web app actually makes against your OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 spec. Import the spec and it's linked as the contract. Then record as usual: a call that breaks the spec shows “Spec mismatch” with the reason, a call the spec doesn't have shows “Not in spec”, and the Spec coverage line above the log counts how many operations you've covered. The same check runs in CI from the command line.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

A call that breaks the linked spec, with the reason.

## Steps

### Import the spec

Import your OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 file, JSON or YAML. Every operation becomes a request you can send, and the spec is linked as the contract.

### Record the flow you test

Press Start Recording and use the app. Calls to the spec's API are checked as they arrive. Calls to other sites, like analytics or fonts, are never judged.

### Read the marks

“Spec mismatch” gives one line of reason, for example "response body $.price: expected number, got string". “Not in spec” marks a call the spec doesn't document. Details lists every problem.

### See what you have not covered

Above the log you'll see "Spec coverage: 3 of 6 operations seen" (open Repeated problems if it's folded). Click it to list the operations you haven't called yet.

### Change or turn off the contract

Settings → Mocks & rules → Pass/fail checks.

## What is checked

Path, method and status must be in the spec, and the parameters, request body, content type, required response headers and response body must match it. Anything RequestFox can't check shows as "not checked", never as a pass.

## The same check in CI

Export the session as JSON (or use a HAR file) and run the command-line tool against the spec. It prints one line per call and the coverage, and exits with 1 on a mismatch:

node requestfox-ci.mjs conform --spec openapi.yaml --session session.json --reporter junit --out results.xml

With --min-coverage 80 it also fails below that share of operations seen. How to get the command-line tool.

## Next

- Run API checks in CI

Saved requests and checks as a pipeline step.

- For API developers

Catch drift between the spec and what ships.

# How to record the HTTPS requests (API calls) a website makes

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-record-api-calls.html

To see the API calls a page makes, open your browser's DevTools, choose Network and filter to Fetch/XHR (XHR in Firefox); nothing to install. To keep them, have the bad ones flagged, and replay or export them, use a browser extension such as RequestFox: install it, open the site, press Start (or Alt Shift S) and use the site as usual. Every fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket frame and server-sent event is listed the moment it starts.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

A recording in progress.

## First, the built-in way: the DevTools Network panel

You don't need an extension to see a page's API calls. In Chrome, open DevTools (F12), choose Network and click the Fetch/XHR filter. Right-click a request and choose Copy to copy it as cURL or as fetch, and tick Preserve log to keep requests across page loads [1]. In Firefox, the Network Monitor opens with Ctrl+Shift+E (Cmd+Opt+E on a Mac) [2]; its XHR button filters the list, and Copy as cURL and Copy as Fetch are in the right-click menu [3].

DevTools lists everything live but leaves the judging to you, and the list is gone when you close it. RequestFox adds the flags, the History and the export. RequestFox vs the DevTools Network panel.

## Steps to record API calls in Chrome, Edge or Firefox

### Install RequestFox

Add it from the Chrome Web Store or Firefox Add-ons. There's nothing to sign up for.

### Open the site you want to test

Any normal web page works. Browser pages, like the extensions page, a new tab or the Web Store, can't be recorded, and RequestFox tells you so if you try.

### Press Start

Click the RequestFox icon to open the side panel (the sidebar in Firefox) and press Start Recording, or press Alt+Shift+S (Option+Shift+S on a Mac). The first time, the browser asks you to allow access to the site: allow it.

### Use the site as usual

Click through the flow you're testing. Each call appears as it starts, tied to the click or form submit that caused it. To record a page's very first calls (sign-in, config, feature flags), tick "Reload the page to record its startup calls" before you press Start Recording.

### Read the flags

Calls that failed, were slow, fired twice or broke inside a 200 OK are marked. Open one to see its headers, body, timing and the reason in plain words.

### Stop, and keep the evidence

Press Stop. The session stays in History, so you can reopen and compare it later. Export it as an HTML report, HAR, CSV or JSON, or copy one call as code.

## Find one call in a long recording

Type in the search box. Every word has to match, in any order, and tokens narrow the list:

- status:500 or method:POST

- host:api.example.com, or -host:cdn.example.com to leave a host out

- path:/users/:id for every call to one endpoint, whatever the id

## If nothing shows up

- The list says to open a site first: you pressed Start on a browser page. Open the site, then press Start.

- You chose not to allow access: press Start again and allow it. You can remove the access later in your browser's settings for the extension.

- The list is empty while recording: the page has made no calls yet. Click something that loads data, or reload the page.

- The shortcut does nothing: another extension may already use it. Set it again at chrome://extensions/shortcuts (Firefox: about:addons, the gear, Manage Extension Shortcuts).

## Sources

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 4 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Firefox Source Docs, "Network Monitor". Checked 4 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

- Firefox Source Docs, "Network request list". Checked 4 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

Something here out of date? Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we'll fix it.

# How to edit and resend a request in Chrome

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-replay-edit-request.html

Record the call with RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, open its card and press Replay to send it again as it was, or choose Edit and send again… in its ··· menu to change the method, address, headers or body first. While recording, the request goes through the page, with its cookies and session. The browsers' own DevTools can do part of this: Chrome resends a request as an editable fetch() call in the Console, and Firefox has Edit and Resend.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

A request opened in Compose, with its response.

## Steps

### Record the call

Press Start Recording in RequestFox and do what makes the call. How to record API calls.

### Open its card

Click the call in the list. Search with filters such as method:POST or status:500 to find it fast.

### Press Replay to send it as it was

The response shows on the card, for example "Replayed → 200 (134 ms)". The secrets redaction hides are still sent, because the replay uses the unredacted copy kept in memory.

### Or change it first: Edit and send again…

In the card's ··· menu, choose Edit and send again…, change the method, address, headers or body, then press Send.

### Keep it for later

Open in Compose, the next item in the same menu, turns it into a request you can save to a collection, use with environments and {{variables}}, and send again any time.

## When the page's CORS rules block it

A replay normally runs as the page. If the API does not allow the page's origin, a GET, HEAD or OPTIONS replay is sent again from the extension by itself; other methods offer "Replay from the extension" first. Sent that way, a request has no page cookies and is marked From extension in the log.

## Outside the browser

Copy as code gives you the same request in 15 languages, cURL for bash and Windows cmd included, plus PowerShell, fetch, Node.js, Python, HTTPie, Go, Java, C#, PHP, Ruby, Swift, Kotlin and Rust.

## Can DevTools resend a request?

Yes, in both browsers, with a different shape. In Chrome, right-click a fetchable request in the Network panel and choose "Edit and resend as fetch". DevTools opens the Console drawer with the request filled in as a fetch() call; edit the call there and press Enter to send it [1]. In Firefox, the Headers tab of the Network Monitor has a Resend button with two items: Resend sends the request again, and Edit and Resend lets you change the method, URL, request headers or body, then Send [2].

What RequestFox adds: the response shows on the call's card and the call stays in the session History; a replay that the page's CORS rules block can be sent from the extension instead; and Open in Compose saves the request to a collection with environments and {{variables}}.

## Sources

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 4 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Firefox Source Docs, "Network request details". Checked 4 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

Something here out of date? Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we will fix it.

# How to clean a HAR file before you share it

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-sanitize-har-file.html

A HAR file is a copy of what your browser sent and received, so it can hold cookies, tokens and passwords. Chrome's Export HAR (sanitized)… leaves out the Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization headers [1]; read the file for anything else. To clean any HAR file, open it in RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox: in History press Open file…, then use the session's More menu, choose HAR and press Export with secrets hidden. The dialog names what was removed.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about browsers are from their own documentation, checked 20 November 2026; sources below.

## What is in a HAR file?

Every request and response the Network panel held when you saved it: addresses, headers, bodies and timing. That includes anything you typed or were given while the panel was open: a sign-in form's password in a request body, a session cookie, a bearer token in a header, a token in an address. Whoever gets the file can read all of it, and a token that has not expired can be used.

## Does Chrome sanitize a HAR file?

Yes, by default. The Network panel's Export HAR (sanitized)… and Save all as HAR (sanitized) omit sensitive data such as the Cookie, Set-Cookie and Authorization headers [1]. To get those back, turn on Allow to generate HAR with sensitive data in Settings, Preferences, Network, and then choose Export HAR (with sensitive data) [1].

The docs name headers. A token in an address, a password in a request body or a card number in a response is a different place, so read the file before you send it. Firefox's Save All As HAR is described in its own docs [2]; do not assume it is cleaned, and clean it as below.

## How do I clean a HAR file with RequestFox?

### Open the file

In RequestFox press History, then Open file… and pick the .har file. While Hide passwords, tokens and card numbers in what is recorded is on in Settings (it is on by default), the tokens, passwords and cookies in it are hidden as it opens. The File opened dialog lists what was hidden, by kind.

### Export it as HAR

On the session, open More and choose HAR. A recording of your own works the same way from Export, bottom right.

### Choose to hide the secrets

If the session still holds a token, a cookie or a password, a dialog titled This file will contain secrets asks first. Its main button, Export with secrets hidden, is the one to press. The question ends with what that export removes: a count of tokens, cookies, passwords, card numbers and file names. Export as it is keeps them.

### Send the new file

The HAR you save has the hidden values written as ***REDACTED***. Keep the original file private.

An export saved when you press Stop is always the hidden copy.

## What should I still check?

- RequestFox hides what looks like a token, cookie, password or card number. A secret written in plain words in a body cannot be told apart from other text, so skim the calls that sign in or pay.

- Personal data is not a secret in this sense. Email addresses, names and ids in responses stay; the Security mark on a card can point at some of them while you record.

To read a file without exporting it, see how to open a HAR file.

## Sources

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 20 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Firefox Source Docs, "Network request list". Checked 20 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

Something here out of date? Tools change. Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we will fix it.

# How to see the API calls a page makes in Firefox, Edge or Safari

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-see-api-calls-firefox-edge-safari.html

Each of these browsers has a Network tool in its built-in developer tools: open the tools, choose Network and use the page. Where you find it differs by browser, so the steps for each are below. If you want to keep the calls after you close the tools, and have the broken ones flagged, use a browser extension. RequestFox is one, for Chrome, Edge and Firefox; Safari is not supported.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about browsers are from their own documentation, checked 20 November 2026; sources below.

## How do I see API calls in Firefox?

- Open the Network Monitor with Ctrl+Shift+E (Cmd+Opt+E on a Mac), or from the Browser Tools menu choose Network [1].

- Use the page. Opening the tool starts monitoring, and it keeps recording while the developer tools stay open [1].

- Filter the list with the XHR button, and right-click a request for Copy as cURL, Copy as Fetch or Save All As HAR [2].

Firefox can also edit a request and send it again with Edit and Resend. API testing in Firefox covers that, plus the add-ons that help.

## How do I see API calls in Microsoft Edge?

- Right-click the page and choose Inspect, or press Ctrl+Shift+J (Command+Option+J on a Mac) [3].

- On the Activity Bar choose the Network tab. If it isn't there, click More tools [3].

- Refresh the page. The Network Log lists each request with its status, type, initiator and time, and you can narrow it with the Filter box or by resource type [3].

The tool logs only after DevTools is open, so open it before you load the page [3]. RequestFox also runs in Edge, as the same extension as in Chrome, if you want the calls kept and flagged.

## How do I see API calls in Safari?

- Turn on the developer tools: choose Safari, then Settings, open Advanced and select Show features for web developers [4].

- A Develop menu now appears in the menu bar, with the developer tools [4].

- Open Web Inspector and choose its Network tab [5].

RequestFox does not run in Safari. In Safari, use the Network tab of Web Inspector to see a page's calls.

## Can I keep the calls and have the broken ones flagged?

Yes, in Chrome, Edge and Firefox. RequestFox is a browser extension that lists the fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket and server-sent events calls a page makes, ties each to the click that caused it, flags the ones that failed, were slow or repeated, and keeps them in History. Press Start Recording, use the page, press Stop. How to record API calls has every step.

RequestFox is in the Chrome Web Store, Microsoft Edge Add-ons and Firefox Add-ons. In Edge it is the same extension as in Chrome. It isn't listed for other browsers, so for those, use the built-in tool above.

## Sources

- Firefox Source Docs, "Network Monitor". Checked 20 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

- Firefox Source Docs, "Network request list". Checked 20 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

- Microsoft Learn, "Inspect network activity". Checked 20 November 2026. learn.microsoft.com

- Apple Support, "Use the developer tools in the Develop menu in Safari". Checked 20 November 2026. support.apple.com

- Apple Support, "Safari Web Inspector Guide: Network tab". Checked 20 November 2026. support.apple.com

# How to slow down or cut off the network for one call or a whole tab

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-slow-down-network.html

Open Mock or break an endpoint in RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, press Add rule, type part of the call's URL and pick a mode: Slow holds the call back for the milliseconds you set, Throttle makes a bigger response take longer, and Network error fails the call as if the server can't be reached. The rule works while RequestFox records. In Chrome, Slow down the whole tab makes one tab load as if on Slow 3G, Fast 3G, 4G or no network at all: the page, its scripts, images and API calls.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 17 November 2026.

## How do I make one API call slow or fail?

### Open Mock or break an endpoint

In RequestFox, open Settings → Mocks & rules → Mock or break an endpoint, and press Add rule….

### Say which call it is for

In URL contains, type part of the call's address, such as /api/search. Leave Method on Any method, or pick one.

### Pick the mode

In Mode, a new rule starts on Mock. Pick Slow and type the Delay ms, such as 4000. Or pick Network error to fail the call with no response at all. Throttle is under More ways: type a speed in KB/s, and the bigger the response, the longer the page waits for it.

### Save it and record

Press Save rule, then Start Recording and use the page. Each call that matches is slowed down or cut off, and the rest go through as usual.

### Watch the page cope

Look for the spinner, the timeout and the error message the page shows. A call cut off by your rule says Simulated on its card, so nobody files it as a real bug.

To make a call fail only some of the time, pick Cycle under More ways and write one step per line, such as pass, pass, offline: the steps take turns, call by call, and start again after the last line.

## How do I slow down a whole tab?

In Chrome, open Settings → Mocks & rules → Slow down the whole tab. Pick a Speed: Slow 3G (2 s delay, 400 kbit/s), Fast 3G (0.56 s delay, 1.4 Mbit/s), 4G (0.17 s delay, 8.1 Mbit/s), Offline, or Custom with your own delay and speeds. Then press Turn on for this tab.

RequestFox uses Chrome's debugger connection to that tab, so the first time, Chrome asks you to allow it, and while it's on, Chrome shows its own "started debugging this browser" bar. Only the speed changes. Nothing is read. One tab is slowed at a time, and it goes back to normal speed when you press Turn off, stop recording, close the tab, close the RequestFox panel or close Chrome's bar.

Firefox can't slow down a whole tab: it has no such API for extensions. There, a Slow or Throttle rule slows the calls you pick.

## Can a slow call stay slow with nothing recording?

Yes, for Slow and Network error. Save the rule with nothing recording, and the line under it offers Keep it on without recording…: press it, and name the site (for example localhost) in the mock set it opens with your rule. The rule then works on that site in every tab, with nothing recording, until you turn the set off. Throttle works only while you record.

## What if the call is not slowed down?

- Nothing is recording. The rules in this list say Works while you record. Press Start Recording, or keep the rule on in a mock set.

- It's a page load, an image or a script. A rule changes the fetch and XMLHttpRequest calls the page makes. In Chrome, slow down the whole tab instead.

- The address doesn't match. Open the call's card and copy part of its URL into URL contains.

- The card's time looks normal. Slow holds the call back before it is sent, and Throttle holds the response back on its way to the page, so the card times only the network part. The page itself still waited.

- Chrome won't slow down the tab. Chrome doesn't let extensions slow down its own pages or the Web Store, and only one tool can debug a tab at a time: close DevTools on that tab, then press Turn on for this tab again.

## Can DevTools do this?

Yes, for the tab it inspects. Chrome's Network panel has a throttling menu with presets such as fast 4G, slow 4G and 3G, an Offline choice and your own profiles [1]. Firefox's network monitor has presets from GPRS to Wi-Fi, and Offline [2]. DevTools slows down everything in that tab. A RequestFox rule slows down or cuts off only the calls you pick, and marks them in the log.

## Sources

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 17 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Firefox Source Docs, "Throttling" (Network Monitor). Checked 17 November 2026. firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org

Something here out of date? Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we'll fix it.

# How to test an MCP server from your browser

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-test-mcp-server.html

In RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, open Compose, set the body type to MCP server, type the server's address (it often ends in /mcp) and press Connect. RequestFox lists the server's tools, resources and prompts. Pick a tool, fill the form it builds from the tool's input schema, and press Call tool to read the response. The requests are plain JSON-RPC over HTTP, and RequestFox runs no AI model: it sends only what you pick.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about the MCP Inspector are from its own documentation, checked 20 November 2026; sources below.

## How do I test an MCP server?

### Choose the MCP server body type

Press Compose in the top bar, open the Body tab and set Body type to MCP server. The tester works over Streamable HTTP, with MCP 2026-07-28 servers and 2025 ones.

### Type the address and connect

Type the server's address in the URL box. It needs to be an http:// or https:// address. Press Connect. The line under it says what RequestFox is asking, then which server you are connected to and which MCP version it speaks.

### Pick a tool, a resource or a prompt

The three lists are Tools, Resources and Prompts, each headed with its count. A tool marked Read-only or Changes data says so. Press Refresh lists if the server's lists changed.

### Fill in the arguments

Under Arguments RequestFox builds a form from the tool's input schema and marks each required field. Edit as JSON switches to raw JSON, and Edit as form back again.

### Call it and read the response

Press Call tool (Read for a resource, Get prompt for a prompt). The badge says Result, Tool error (the tool ran and reported an error) or an error code from the server. If the tool has an output schema, RequestFox says whether the result matches it. The Messages list under the result shows everything that went over the wire.

## Can I copy what was sent?

Yes. Under a result press Copy as request. The dialog shows the JSON-RPC request RequestFox sent for that call, with secrets hidden, and offers it as Copy as cURL or Copy as JSON. Paste it into a bug report, or run the cURL command to reproduce the call outside the browser.

## What if it does not connect?

- Nothing answers. Is the server running, and is the address right? RequestFox says the server did not answer. A 404 usually means the path: it often ends in /mcp.

- The server wants a sign-in (HTTP 401). Press Sign in… to sign in with the server's own sign-in server, or set a token in the Auth tab. RequestFox asks before it goes to a sign-in server, and says at which step a sign-in stopped.

- HTTP 403. Check the Auth tab. A server on your own computer may also refuse the browser's Origin header; allow it in the server.

- You are offline, or RequestFox has no permission for the site. It says so; allow the site when the browser asks, then connect again.

- An old server. If the server does not answer a POST, RequestFox tries the older HTTP+SSE transport (2024-11-05) before it gives up.

## Should I use RequestFox or the MCP Inspector?

The MCP Inspector is the project's reference tool for testing and debugging MCP servers. It runs through npx on your computer, in a browser, on the command line or in a terminal, and it can launch a local server by its command [1]. It needs Node.js [1].

RequestFox is already in your browser, and it tests servers that answer over HTTP. It cannot start a stdio server: a stdio server is a program, and a browser cannot start one. Use the Inspector for that. For a server on a web address, the two do the same jobs; RequestFox keeps the call beside your other requests, environments and sign-ins.

## Sources

- Model Context Protocol, "MCP Inspector". Checked 20 November 2026. modelcontextprotocol.io

Something here out of date? Tools change. Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we will fix it.

# How to test a server-sent events (SSE) endpoint in the browser

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-test-server-sent-events.html

In RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, open Compose, type the endpoint's address and press Send. A server-sent events response stays open: the status line says Streaming… with a count of events, each event is listed as it arrives, and Stop ends the read and keeps what came. On a recorded call, RequestFox flags a stream that sent an error event, one that closed without its end marker, and one that went quiet for a long time. Headers and auth go in like any other request.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. The event stream format is from the HTML standard, checked 20 November 2026; source below.

## How do I test a server-sent events endpoint?

### Open Compose and type the address

Press Compose in the top bar, choose the method (usually GET) and type the endpoint's address. Add the headers the server wants, such as an Authorization header, in the Headers tab, or set the auth in the Auth tab.

### Press Send

Press Send. When the response is an event stream, the status line says Streaming… with the number of events so far, and the events fill in below it.

### Stop when you have seen enough

Press Stop on the status line. RequestFox ends the read and keeps the events up to that point; the line says the status and how many events were kept.

### Read the events

Each event shows its fields. For a language model's token stream, the label Token stream shows, with the text the tokens add up to under Text. A long stream keeps its newest events within the body limit, and a note says how many are shown.

## What does RequestFox flag in a stream?

- Stream error: the stream sent an error event inside its 200 OK (an event: error, or an event whose JSON is an error). The card shows the error's own message.

- Ended early: a stream with a known end marker, such as the [DONE] of a language model's stream, closed without it, so the response may be cut off. It is checked only for streams RequestFox recognises as that kind.

- A paused badge, with the longest gap: the stream stopped sending for a long time between two events. The note says the longest pause and how many pauses of 5 seconds or more there were.

These flags are on the call's card in the log, for streams a page reads while you record. An event stream is text with the type text/event-stream; events are separated by a blank line, and the fields are event, data, id and retry [1]. A browser drops a last event that has no blank line after it [1], and RequestFox says so on that row.

## Can I see the events my own page receives?

Yes. Press Start Recording and use the page. A stream it reads with fetch, XMLHttpRequest or EventSource stays open as a row that fills as events arrive, and is kept when you stop. Connections the page opened before you pressed Start are not seen: reload the page. WebSocket / SSE activity in the top bar lists the page's socket and event-stream messages. For an EventSource, the rows are the event types the page listens for: the browser hands a page no others.

## What if no events show?

- The response is not an event stream. A server has to answer with the type text/event-stream [1]; check the response headers on the card.

- The server sends events only when something happens. The status line keeps saying Streaming… until the server sends one, or you press Stop.

- It stopped on its own. The card says why: the stream broke off with a network error, the page closed it, or recording stopped while it was open.

- A last event is missing. If the server did not end it with a blank line, a browser drops it [1].

## Sources

- WHATWG, HTML Standard, "Server-sent events". Checked 20 November 2026. html.spec.whatwg.org

Something here out of date? Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we will fix it.

# How to test a WebSocket or Socket.IO server in the browser

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/guide-test-websocket.html

Open WebSocket / SSE activity in RequestFox, a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox, type the server's ws:// or wss:// URL under Open a connection and press Connect. Type a message and press Send. Whatever the server sends back shows below, each line marked Received or Sent. For a Socket.IO server, pick Socket.IO beside the URL: RequestFox joins the namespace, answers the pings for you, and sends events with Emit. If the connection closes, it tells you the close code and what it means.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 17 November 2026.

## How do I connect to a WebSocket server?

### Open WebSocket / SSE activity

In RequestFox, press WebSocket / SSE activity in the top bar. Open a connection is the box at the bottom.

### Type the URL and press Connect

Type the server's address, such as wss://api.example.com/socket; {{variables}} work in it. Press Connect. The line under it says Connecting…, then which server you're connected to.

### Add a header or subprotocol if the server needs one

Headers (optional) go with the handshake in Chrome and Firefox, such as Authorization: Bearer {{token}}; the browser may ask you to allow RequestFox on that site. Subprotocol (optional) takes names separated by commas.

### Send a message

Type it and press Send. Send as picks Text, Binary (base64) or Binary (hex). Save message keeps one to send again later.

### Read what came back

Each line says Received or Sent. Filter messages narrows the list, and Copy log copies it for a bug report. Tick Reconnect if it drops for RequestFox to try again after a drop, up to five times.

Need a second socket at the same time, such as two users in one chat? Press New connection: up to five connections stay open side by side, each with its own URL, headers and log.

## How do I test a Socket.IO server?

A Socket.IO server speaks its own protocol on top of WebSocket (a handshake, pings, namespaces and events), so pick Socket.IO in the list beside the URL instead of WebSocket. An http:// or https:// address works too. Then set the Path (usually /socket.io/), the Namespace, the Server version (v3 / v4, or v2 for an older server) and, if the server checks one, the Auth payload (JSON, optional).

After Connect, type an Event name and its Arguments (JSON), tick Wait for ack if the server answers the event, and press Emit. RequestFox answers the server's pings itself and keeps them out of the way until you press Show pings. It talks Socket.IO over WebSocket only: long-polling isn't supported.

## Can I see the sockets my web app opens?

Yes. Press Start Recording and use the page: every WebSocket and server-sent events connection it opens shows under Recorded activity, with each message. A connection the page opened before you pressed Start isn't seen, so reload the page. Socket.IO frames read as events with their arguments, and Raw frames shows them as sent. While recording, Inject a message pushes a message into the page's open connection, as if the server had sent it.

## What if it does not connect?

- "Couldn't connect": check the URL and that the server is running. A WebSocket address starts with ws:// or wss://.

- "The server answered HTTP 401" (or 403, 404) to the handshake: the URL is wrong, or the server wants a token or a sign-in. Add the header it expects, or for Socket.IO the auth payload.

- It closes with a code. RequestFox says what the code means: 1006 is a drop with no close message (network, proxy or server crash), 1008 is refused by the server's rules (often sign-in), 1011 is a server error.

- Socket.IO never joins. Check that the server runs Socket.IO and that Server version matches it.

- The headers couldn't be added. Allow RequestFox on that site when the browser asks, then press Connect again: nothing is sent without them.

## Sources

A web page's own WebSocket takes only the address and the subprotocols [1]; it can't set other headers, which is why RequestFox adds them to the handshake for you.

- MDN Web Docs, "WebSocket: WebSocket() constructor". Checked 17 November 2026. developer.mozilla.org

Something here out of date? Tell us at the address in the privacy policy and we'll fix it.

## Keyboard shortcuts

- Alt Shift S: Start or stop recording; opens the panel

- Alt Shift M: Switch the panel to Full, Background or Mini

- /: Jump to the search box

- F6 (back: Shift F6): Move to the next part of the panel: top bar, start bar, filters, calls, footer

- Ctrl Enter (Mac: Cmd Enter): Send from any Compose field

- Ctrl S (Mac: Cmd S): Save the request in Compose: changes go into the saved request; a new one opens Save to collection

- Esc: Close a dialog or menu, or the open panel, and go back where you were

- Enter in Compose's address: Send

On a Mac, use Option+Shift instead of Alt+Shift. In the panel, Help → Keyboard shortcuts lists them. Change the first two at chrome://extensions/shortcuts (Firefox: about:addons, the gear, Manage Extension Shortcuts).

# RequestFox vs Bruno

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-bruno.html

Pick Bruno if you want your API requests as plain files in Git, next to your code, in an offline-first desktop client. Pick RequestFox if you'd rather start from what your web app actually sends in the browser, with problems flagged while you test. Neither needs an account, and RequestFox imports Bruno collections.

Facts about Bruno are from its own documentation, checked 4 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## Side by side

|

| | RequestFox | Bruno

| What it is | A browser extension that records and tests the calls a web app makes | A Git-friendly, offline-first API client [1]

| Account | None | Not required [1]

| Where requests live | In your browser; in Chrome, a linked folder can hold them as files too | Files in your collection folder, requests in YAML, to version in Git [1]

| Calls your web app makes | Recorded as you click, with problems flagged | You write the requests

| CI | A one-file CLI exported from the panel: assert, run, conform and loadtest, over HTTP/2 if you ask | Bruno CLI runs collections from the terminal [2]

| Price | Free, no paid tier | No account needed; an email is asked for only if you buy a licence key [1]

## Where Bruno is stronger

- Requests as readable files you review like code, in Git [1].

- It's a desktop client, so a web page's CORS rules never apply.

- NTLM and Akamai EdgeGrid auth [3], which RequestFox doesn't have.

## Where RequestFox is different

- Nothing to write first: it records what the app sent, in the session you're already signed in to.

- It flags problems as they happen and ties each one to the click that caused it.

- Mock and fault rules change the responses your app gets, right in the browser.

## Requests as files, in Chrome too

In Chrome, Compose → Export → Link a folder… writes your saved requests, environments, suites, checks and rules as files to a folder you pick, and keeps them up to date there, so they can live in Git next to the code. To bring Bruno collections over, use Compose → Import → Import a collection….

## Sources

- Bruno Docs, "Getting Started" (what Bruno is). Checked 4 November 2026. docs.usebruno.com

- Bruno Docs, home: Bruno CLI and Licensing. Checked 4 November 2026. docs.usebruno.com

- Bruno Docs, "Authentication" overview. Checked 4 November 2026. docs.usebruno.com
