# RequestFox vs the DevTools Network panel

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-devtools.html

Use the DevTools Network panel for a raw, live view of everything one page loads, with nothing to install. Use RequestFox when you test a flow and want the API problems pointed out, each tied to your click, kept in History and ready to mock, replay or export.

Facts about DevTools are from Chrome's own documentation, checked 4 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## Side by side

|

| | RequestFox | DevTools Network panel

| What it lists | API calls: fetch, XMLHttpRequest, WebSocket, server-sent events, EventSource streams; as cards, a sortable table or a session Overview | Every resource the page loads [1]

| Keeps the list | Every session, in History, to reopen and compare | Across page loads with Preserve log [2]

| Finding problems | Flags failed, slow, duplicate and retried calls, N+1, errors inside a 200, expired tokens, changed shapes | You filter and read: by domain, status code and other properties, or inverted [2]

| Changing responses | Mock, fail, slow, throttle or pause a call, or in Chrome slow the whole tab; labelled in the log | Local overrides of content and response headers, saved in a folder you choose [3]

| Export | HTML report, HAR, CSV, JSON, Postman, Bruno, Insomnia, Hoppscotch, an API docs page, OpenAPI 3.0, tests, code in 15 languages | HAR (sensitive headers left out), Copy as cURL and as fetch [2]

| Browsers | Chrome, Edge and Firefox | Chrome (Firefox has its own Network Monitor)

## Where DevTools is stronger

- It is already there: nothing to install, no site access to allow.

- It shows every resource (scripts, styles, images, fonts), not only API calls [1].

- Network throttling and request blocking for the whole page [1], built in and with nothing to allow. RequestFox's whole-tab throttle is Chrome only, optional and shows Chrome's own debugging bar.

- Its EventStream tab filters an open stream's events with a regular expression [2]; RequestFox filters its rows with the log's search.

## What RequestFox adds

- Problems are pointed out instead of found by eye, with the reason in plain words.

- Each call is tied to the click or form submit that caused it.

- Sessions survive closing DevTools and the browser, and two runs can be compared.

- Per-endpoint checks, an OpenAPI contract, suites and a CLI for CI.

- Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields redacted by default in what you view and export.

How to record API calls with RequestFox.

## Copy a call as code

DevTools copies a request as cURL or as fetch [2]. RequestFox copies any recorded or composed request as code in 15 languages, cURL for bash and Windows cmd included, and keeps {{variables}} that hold secrets as written.

- Chrome for Developers, "Network features reference". Checked 4 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

- Chrome for Developers, "Override web content and HTTP response headers locally". Checked 4 November 2026. developer.chrome.com

# RequestFox vs Hoppscotch

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-hoppscotch.html

Pick Hoppscotch if you want an open-source API client on the web, desktop or CLI that your team can self-host, with WebSocket, SSE, Socket.IO and MQTT clients [3]. Pick RequestFox to record and judge the calls your own web app makes while you test it. RequestFox imports Hoppscotch collections.

Facts about Hoppscotch are from its own documentation, checked 4 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## Side by side

|

| | RequestFox | Hoppscotch

| Where it runs | A side panel in Chrome and Edge, a sidebar in Firefox | Web, Mac, Windows, Linux and CLI; the web app needs no install [1]

| Self-hosting | Nothing to host: there is no server | Host it on your own server for your team [1]

| Calls your web app makes | Recorded as you click, with problems flagged | You build the requests

| CORS from the web app | Sends through the page while recording, or from the extension itself | An interceptor: the Hoppscotch Agent, a proxy or the browser extension [2]

| Realtime clients | WebSocket and Socket.IO client; WebSocket, Socket.IO and SSE recorded, with live rows for fetch, XMLHttpRequest and EventSource streams | WebSocket, SSE, Socket.IO and MQTT [3]

| Source | Free; MIT licence, repository not public | Source code open and auditable [1]

## Where Hoppscotch is stronger

- Open source, and you can self-host it for a team [1].

- An MQTT client [3]. RequestFox has none.

- It runs on the web with nothing to install [1].

## Where RequestFox is different

- It records what your app actually sends and flags the problems, each tied to the click that caused it.

- Mock and fault rules change the responses your app receives.

- History keeps every session, so you can compare runs and export evidence for a bug report.

## Sockets and streams in the browser

While you record, RequestFox lists the page's own WebSocket frames and server-sent events next to its other calls, and reads Socket.IO frames as events with their arguments. Its WebSocket client connects to any ws:// or wss:// server, has a Socket.IO mode, and keeps the messages you save.

# RequestFox vs Insomnia

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-insomnia.html

Pick Insomnia if you want an open-source desktop client to design, debug and test APIs, with plugins, mock servers and a choice of local, Git or cloud storage. Pick RequestFox if you need to test the calls a web app makes in the browser, with problems flagged as they happen. RequestFox imports Insomnia exports.

Facts about Insomnia are from its own documentation, checked 4 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## Side by side

|

| | RequestFox | Insomnia

| Where it runs | A side panel in Chrome and Edge, a sidebar in Firefox | Desktop app for macOS, Windows and Ubuntu [1]

| Storage and account | In your browser; no account | Local Vault (on your device), Scratch Pad (before logging in), Git Sync, or Cloud Sync [2]

| Calls your web app makes | Recorded as you click, with problems flagged | You build the requests

| Mocking | Mock, fail, slow or pause calls your app makes, in the browser; mock sets that stay on, and in Chrome a script can rewrite a request or response | Mock servers that simulate endpoints, including cloud-hosted ones [1]

| CI | A one-file CLI exported from the panel | Inso CLI [1]

| Extending it | No plugins (no third-party code) | Plugins [1]

| Source | Free; MIT licence, repository not public | Open source [1]

## Where Insomnia is stronger

- It's open source, and you can extend it with plugins [1].

- You choose where requests live, from local only to Git and cloud sync for teams [2].

- Mock servers that other people and services can call [1].

## Where RequestFox is different

- It works on what your app actually sends, in the session you're signed in to.

- It flags failed, slow, duplicate and silently broken calls as you test, tied to your click.

- Nothing to install outside the browser, and no account for anything.

- It imports Insomnia exports (v4 JSON and v5 YAML) and exports your collections as Insomnia v5 YAML, so your requests come with you and can go back.

## Bring your Insomnia requests, then run them in CI

Start with Compose → Import → Import a collection… and pick your Insomnia export (v4 JSON or v5 YAML). Chain the requests into a suite, then use Export as CI config: you get a config file and a one-file command-line tool for your pipeline.

How to run API checks in CI.

# RequestFox vs Postman

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-postman.html

RequestFox is a free Postman alternative that runs in the browser, though not a full replacement. Pick Postman if you need to design, document and share APIs across a team, with many protocols and shared workspaces. Pick RequestFox if you want to test the API calls a real web app makes in the browser, with problems flagged for you and nothing to sign in to. The two work together: RequestFox imports and exports Postman collections.

Facts about Postman are from its own documentation, checked 4 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## Side by side

|

| | RequestFox | Postman

| Where it runs | A side panel in Chrome and Edge, a sidebar in Firefox | Desktop app and web app [1]

| Without an account | Everything | The lightweight API Client builds and sends requests and keeps history; collections and environments need a workspace, which needs an account [2]

| Calls your web app makes | Recorded as you click, each flagged if it failed, dragged, fired twice or broke inside a 200 OK | Postman Interceptor, a browser extension, captures browser requests and cookies into Postman while the app is open [1]

| Protocols for your own requests | HTTP (REST, GraphQL, SOAP), WebSocket and Socket.IO; gRPC-Web and Connect with your .proto files; MCP servers; server-sent events recorded | HTTP, WebSocket, Socket.IO, GraphQL, gRPC and MQTT [2]

| Team sharing | As files: collections, sessions, HAR, reports | Workspaces [2]

## Is there still a Postman Chrome app?

No. On 1 November 2017 Postman said Chrome apps were being deprecated and that new features would go only to its native apps, for Windows, Mac and Linux [3]. Today Postman runs as a desktop app and a web app, and its browser extension, Interceptor, captures browser requests and cookies and sends them to Postman [1].

RequestFox isn't a copy of that app, and it's not a team workspace. It's a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox that records and judges the calls your own web app makes. It has no cloud sync and no gRPC or MQTT client (gRPC-Web and Connect only); you share work as files.

## Where Postman is stronger

- Team work: collections and environments live in workspaces you can share [2].

- More protocols: gRPC and MQTT clients [2]. RequestFox sends gRPC-Web and Connect only, and has no MQTT client.

- As a desktop app, it isn't bound by a web page's CORS rules.

## Where RequestFox is different

- It starts from what your app actually sends, in the session you're signed in to, so there's nothing to retype.

- It judges the calls: failed, slow, duplicate and retried requests, N+1 bursts, GraphQL errors in a 200, expired tokens and changed shapes are flagged as they happen.

- Mock and fault rules change the responses your app gets, labelled so nobody files them as bugs. Mock sets stay on with nothing recording, and in Chrome a script can rewrite a request or response.

- No account for anything, and nothing is sent to us.

## Use both

Import your Postman collections (v2.0 and v2.1) into RequestFox to send them from the browser, and export a recorded session or your saved collections as a Postman collection to keep working in Postman. Record the calls first.

## Move a Postman collection into RequestFox

RequestFox reads Postman collection files (v2.0 and v2.1) and keeps what it can use.

- Open Compose, then Import → Import a collection…, and pick the file.

- RequestFox saves it as a collection of its own and says what it kept: variables and auth in the collection's settings, and the tests it turned into checks and chaining.

- Scripts it couldn't turn into checks are listed by name, so nothing is dropped silently.

- Send any request from the collection, or copy it as code.

Step by step, with the tests that come along and what to set up again: how to import a Postman collection.

- Postman Learning Center, "Build and send requests offline using the lightweight Postman API Client". Checked 4 November 2026. learning.postman.com

- Postman Blog, "Goodbye Postman Chrome app", 1 November 2017. Checked 4 November 2026. blog.postman.com

# RequestFox or a proxy tool: HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman and Charles

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-proxy-tools.html

RequestFox is a browser extension: it sees the calls a web app makes in a Chrome, Edge or Firefox tab, with nothing else to set up. HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman and Charles are apps you install on your computer that sit between your apps and the internet: they see the traffic of whatever you send through them, phones and desktop apps included, once that app or device trusts their certificate for HTTPS. Pick a proxy tool when the traffic isn't in a browser tab. Pick RequestFox when it is, and you'd like the broken calls flagged for you, with no certificate, no proxy setting and no account.

Facts about HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman and Charles are from their own pages, checked 15 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## How do they compare, side by side?

|

| | RequestFox | HTTP Toolkit | Proxyman | Charles

| What it is | A browser extension that records and judges the calls a web app makes, and lets you replay, mock, check and export them | An open-source app for debugging, testing and building with HTTP, on Windows, Linux and Mac [1] | A native macOS app to capture, decrypt and mock HTTP(S) traffic; its page also lists Windows, Linux, iOS and Android [4] | An HTTP proxy, HTTP monitor and reverse proxy for Windows, macOS and Linux [6]

| Whose traffic it sees | The browser tabs you record, in Chrome, Edge and Firefox | Android and iOS apps, whole devices, Docker containers, browser windows, terminals and backend processes [1][2] | iOS and Android devices and the iOS Simulator, with standalone iOS and Android apps [4] | The HTTP and HTTPS traffic between your machine and the internet; iOS devices and simulators once they trust its certificate [6][9]

| HTTPS | Read inside the browser: no certificate to trust, no proxy to set | Captured; a client you set up by hand must trust its certificate [1][2] | Decrypted and shown in plain text [4] | SSL proxying shows it in plain text; each device must trust the Charles root certificate, and on Android only apps you control [7][9]

| Changing traffic | Mock, fail, slow down or pause one call for editing; header and URL rules; in Chrome, a script that rewrites a request or response | Request and response breakpoints in the free plan; automatic rewrite rules, mock responses, errors and timeouts in Pro [3] | Breakpoints, Map Local and JavaScript scripts [4], in the paid licences; the free trial leaves them out [5] | Breakpoints, Map Local, Map Remote, Rewrite, and slower connections with the bandwidth and latency you set [7][8]

| Price | Free, with no paid tier | A free Hobbyist plan; Professional and Team plans are paid [3] | A free trial with limited features; licences from $89 for one device, paid once, with a year of updates [5] | A 30-day trial; $50 a licence when you buy one to four [10]

## Where are the proxy tools stronger?

- Traffic from outside the browser: phones, simulators, desktop apps, Docker containers and terminals [1][4][6].

- HTTPS from any app or device that trusts their certificate, mobile apps included [2][4][9].

- One place to change the traffic of every app at once: breakpoints in all three [3][4][7], Map Local in Proxyman and Charles [4][8], Rewrite and Map Remote in Charles [8].

- Charles slows the whole connection, with the bandwidth and latency you choose [7].

- HTTP Toolkit is open source, according to its own page [1].

## Where is RequestFox different?

- Nothing to set up but the extension: no certificate to trust, no proxy setting, and the rest of your computer's traffic is left alone.

- It judges the calls. Failed, slow, duplicate and retried requests, N+1 bursts, GraphQL errors in a 200, expired tokens and changed shapes are flagged as they happen, each tied to the click that caused it.

- It keeps every session, so you can compare today's run with yesterday's, and turns a recording into checks you can run in CI.

- Mock and fault rules label the calls they change, so nobody files a mocked response as a bug.

- No account for anything, and nothing is sent to us.

Where RequestFox falls short, so you're not surprised:

- It sees what a browser tab sends, in Chrome, Edge and Firefox: not a phone, a desktop app or a terminal.

- Slowing a whole tab works in Chrome only; Firefox offers each rule's Slow and Throttle modes instead.

- Rewriting a request or response with a script runs in Chrome only.

- It is free. Its code is MIT-licensed and ships readable inside the extension, so you can check it yourself; the source repository is not public.

## Can I use both?

Yes. They do different jobs. Use a proxy tool for the phone build or the desktop app, and RequestFox for the web app in the browser, where it flags the broken calls and turns a flow into checks. How to record the API calls a web app makes. Also: RequestFox vs Requestly and RequestFox vs the DevTools Network panel.

- HTTP Toolkit, home page. Checked 15 November 2026. httptoolkit.com

- HTTP Toolkit docs, "Intercepting". Checked 15 November 2026. httptoolkit.com

- HTTP Toolkit, "Pricing". Checked 15 November 2026. httptoolkit.com

- Proxyman, home page. Checked 15 November 2026. proxyman.com

- Proxyman, "Pricing". Checked 15 November 2026. proxyman.com

- Charles, home page. Checked 15 November 2026. charlesproxy.com

- Charles, "About Charles". Checked 15 November 2026. charlesproxy.com

- Charles documentation, "Tools". Checked 15 November 2026. charlesproxy.com

- Charles documentation, "SSL Certificates". Checked 15 November 2026. charlesproxy.com

- Charles, "Buy". Checked 15 November 2026. charlesproxy.com

# RequestFox vs Requestly: two browser extensions for working with API calls

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-requestly.html

RequestFox and Requestly are both browser extensions that work with the API calls a web app makes. Pick Requestly if you want to intercept and rewrite traffic with rules, in many browsers and, with its desktop app, beyond the browser. Pick RequestFox if you want to record the calls a web app makes, have the broken ones flagged for you, and test them, with no account and nothing sent to us. They do different jobs, and some people run both.

Facts about Requestly are from its own pages, checked 4 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## How do they compare, side by side?

|

| | RequestFox | Requestly

| What it is | A browser extension that records and judges the calls a web app makes, and lets you replay, mock, check and export them | A browser extension that intercepts and changes browser traffic with rules [2]. It is also an API client, and a BrowserStack product [5]

| Rules that change traffic | Mock and fault rules for an endpoint; header and URL rules that can stay on with nothing recording; in Chrome, a script that rewrites a request or response | Rules that modify headers, bodies and query parameters, redirect, replace strings, delay, cancel, map to local or remote files, change the user agent, and insert scripts [1]

| Watching traffic | Every call is recorded, tied to the click that caused it and kept in History; failed, slow, duplicate and retried calls, N+1 bursts and errors inside a 200 OK are flagged | A network traffic table, session recording and HAR import [1]

| Browsers | Chrome, Edge and Firefox | Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Brave, Arc, Vivaldi and Opera; Safari with fewer features [1][2]

| Beyond the browser | Browser tabs only | With its desktop app: mobile devices, simulators, desktop apps, Node.js and the terminal [1]

| Team sharing | As files: collections, sessions, HAR, reports | Team Workspaces [1]

| Price | Free, with no paid tier | Its HTTP Interceptor page says "Free to use" [3]; its pricing page lists plans for the API platform from $10 per user per month, billed annually, with a 30-day trial [4]

| Source code | Free; MIT licence, repository not public | Its HTTP Interceptor page calls it open source [3]

## Where is Requestly stronger?

- A long list of rule types that stay on while you browse: change headers or bodies, redirect to another environment, map a URL to a local file, insert your own script or style into a page [1].

- More browsers: its extension lists Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Brave, Arc, Vivaldi and Opera [1].

- Traffic from outside the browser, through its desktop app: phones, simulators, desktop apps, Node.js and the terminal [1].

- Team Workspaces that sync rules between the extension and the desktop app [1].

- A wider product: a Git-native API client with collections, scripts and tests, sold in team plans [4][5].

## Where is RequestFox different?

- It judges the calls. Failed, slow, duplicate and retried requests, N+1 bursts, GraphQL errors in a 200, expired tokens and changed shapes are flagged as they happen, each tied to the click that caused it.

- It keeps every session, so you can compare today's run with yesterday's, and turns a recording into checks you can run in CI.

- No account for anything, and nothing is sent to us.

- Mock and fault rules label the calls they change, so nobody files a mocked response as a bug.

Where RequestFox falls short, so you're not surprised:

- It runs in Chrome, Edge and Firefox, and only sees what a browser tab sends. Mobile and desktop apps need a proxy tool such as HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman or Charles.

- It has no rule that puts script or style into a page.

- There's no team workspace or cloud sync, by design. You share work as files.

- It is free. Its code is MIT-licensed and ships readable inside the extension, so you can check it yourself; the source repository is not public.

## Can I use both?

Yes. They're separate extensions with separate jobs. Record and test a flow in RequestFox to see which calls fail and why, and keep always-on rewrites, like sending a request to a staging server, in Requestly. How to mock an API response in RequestFox. Also: RequestFox vs the DevTools Network panel and RequestFox vs Postman.

# RequestFox vs Thunder Client: a browser extension or an editor extension

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare-thunder-client.html

Thunder Client is a REST API client that lives inside your code editor, VS Code or a JetBrains IDE [2]. RequestFox is a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox that records the calls a web app makes, flags the broken ones and lets you send, mock and export them. Pick Thunder Client if you want to write and keep requests beside your code, with Git Sync on a paid plan. Pick RequestFox if you want to see what your web app actually sends, with no account, no plan limits and nothing sent to us.

Facts about Thunder Client are from its own pages, checked 20 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## How do they compare, side by side?

|

| | RequestFox | Thunder Client

| Where it runs | In Chrome, Edge and Firefox, beside the page you test | Inside the editor: VS Code, and JetBrains IDEs [2]

| What it starts from | The calls your web app makes, recorded and flagged | Requests you test from your editor [2]

| Free plan | Free, with no paid tier and no limit by plan | Free: 50 requests per collection and 50 collection runs per user, a local monthly limit; runs in CI/CD have no limit [1]

| Paid plans | None | Starter $3, Business $7, Enterprise $16 per user per month, billed annually [1]

| Git and teams | No cloud sync, by design: share collections, sessions, HAR and reports as files | Git Sync, from the Starter plan [1][2]

| Scripting | Pre-request and post-response scripts run in Chrome only; chaining values between requests works in both browsers | Custom scripting, from the Starter plan [1]

| Where data lives | On your computer; nothing is sent to us | Requests and data stay on your machine [2]

## Where is Thunder Client stronger?

- It's in your editor, so you can test an API without switching windows [2].

- It supports JetBrains IDEs as well as VS Code and its forks [2].

- Git Sync saves collections to a repository for team sharing, and Starter adds global environments, scripting and data-driven testing [1][2].

- It has its own MCP server that lets AI agents create, run and test requests [2].

## Where is RequestFox different?

- It watches the real traffic. Failed, slow, duplicate and retried calls, N+1 bursts and errors inside a 200 OK are flagged as they happen, each tied to the click that caused it.

- It's free with no paid tier, so there's no request cap to hit.

- You mock a call right from its own card, and it's labelled so nobody files it as a bug. How to mock an API response.

- No account for anything, and nothing is sent to us.

Where RequestFox falls short: it only sees what a browser tab sends, it has no team workspace, and it isn't in your editor. For many people the two fit together: write requests in the editor, and use RequestFox to see what the page itself sends.

## Can I bring my Thunder Client requests into RequestFox?

Yes. In Compose, open Import and press Import a collection…. It reads Thunder Client exports. The import guide shows what comes across. See also tools that need no login and the comparison with Postman.

# Which API tool fits which job

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/compare.html

Each of these tools is the right pick for some job. RequestFox is the one that watches the web app you are testing and points out the API problems as they happen. For designing and sharing APIs across a team, a desktop client such as Postman, Insomnia, Bruno or Hoppscotch fits better, and RequestFox imports from all four.

Facts about other tools come from their own documentation, linked on each page. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## The short answer

- Testing a web app and want problems found for you: RequestFox.

- A raw look at everything one page load does, nothing to install: the DevTools Network panel.

- Designing, documenting and sharing APIs across a team: Postman or Insomnia.

- API requests kept as plain files in Git, next to the code: Bruno.

- An open-source client on the web you can self-host: Hoppscotch.

- Rules that redirect, rewrite or inject on every page, all the time: Requestly.

- Traffic from a phone, a desktop app or the terminal: a proxy tool such as HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman or Charles.

## Each comparison

- RequestFox vs Postman

Browser recording and flags, or team workspaces and more protocols.

- RequestFox vs DevTools Network

The judging and the history, or the raw live view.

- RequestFox vs Insomnia

In the browser, or an open-source desktop client with plugins.

- RequestFox vs Bruno

Record what the app sent, or write requests as files in Git.

- RequestFox vs Hoppscotch

Your app's real calls, or a self-hostable client with realtime protocols.

- RequestFox vs Requestly

Two browser extensions: record and flag the calls, or intercept and rewrite them.

- RequestFox vs proxy tools

A browser tab, with nothing to set up, or any app through a proxy: HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman, Charles.

- RequestFox vs Postman Interceptor

Record in the browser on its own, or hand the traffic to Postman.

- Postman alternative, no login

A free alternative with no account at all, and what Insomnia, Thunder Client and Postman say on their own pricing pages.

- RequestFox vs Thunder Client

Your web app's real calls in the browser, or requests kept in your editor: free limits and prices from their pages.

## Where RequestFox falls short

Honest limits of RequestFox 2.5.0, so you are not surprised:

- It sees what a browser tab sends. Mobile and desktop apps need a proxy tool such as HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman or Charles.

- While recording, Compose sends from the page you are testing, with its cookies; with nothing recording it sends from the extension itself, without any page's cookies, after the browser asks once for that site.

- No team workspace or cloud sync, by design. Share work as files: collections, sessions, HAR and reports.

- An EventSource stream's live rows are the event types the page listens for: the browser hands a page no others.

- Pre-request and post-response scripts, and rewriting a request or response with a script, run in Chrome only: Firefox does not let extensions run code typed at runtime. Chaining values between requests works in both.

- No native gRPC or MQTT client (gRPC-Web and Connect only).

- It is free. Its code is MIT-licensed and ships readable inside the extension, so you can check it yourself; the source repository is not public.

## Try it on the app you are testing today.

Free, in Chrome, Edge and Firefox.

# A Postman alternative with no login

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/postman-alternative-no-login.html

RequestFox is a browser extension for Chrome, Edge and Firefox with no account to make, no sign-in and no server of ours: install it and send a request. It's free, with no paid tier. Insomnia's Scratch Pad is another local-only way to work without logging in [2]. Below is what each vendor's own pricing page says about price and accounts, and where it says nothing.

Facts about other tools are from their own pricing pages, checked 20 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team, for RequestFox 2.5.0.

## Which tools need an account?

|

| | RequestFox | Postman | Insomnia | Thunder Client

| Free plan | Free, no paid tier | Free, one user included [1] | Essentials, $0 [2] | Free, 50 requests per collection [3]

| Account | None to make | Free is offered through a sign-up button; the page does not say whether an account is required [1] | A local-only Scratch Pad that works without logging in [2] | The Free plan has a sign-up button; the page says collections and environments are stored locally [3]

| Paid plans | None | Solo $9, Team $19 per user per month, billed annually [1] | Pro $12, Enterprise $45 per user per month [2] | Starter $3, Business $7, Enterprise $16 per user per month [3]

## What do the other tools' pages say?

- Postman: Free is "for individuals", with one user [1]. The pricing page doesn't say whether you can use the apps without signing in, so check its account documentation before you rely on that.

- Insomnia: the pricing page describes a "local-only, free forever Scratch Pad" you can use without logging in. Its Essentials plan is free and includes Git Sync for up to 3 users and 1,000 mock server requests a month [2].

- Thunder Client: the Free plan caps a collection at 50 requests and leaves out Git Sync, custom scripting and data-driven testing, which start at Starter [3].

- Bruno: the Open Source plan is $0 and includes the API client, testing, scripting, code generation and unlimited collection runs. Its pricing page says nothing about accounts [4].

## What is RequestFox, and what is it not?

RequestFox sits in your browser beside the page you're testing. It records the calls the page makes, flags the ones that failed, were slow or repeated, and lets you send, edit, mock and export them. It's free, with no paid tier, and nothing is sent to us. For the full comparison, see RequestFox vs Postman.

It isn't a team workspace. There's no cloud sync, by design, so you share work as files (collections, sessions, HAR and reports). It sees what a browser tab sends, not a phone or desktop app. If your team needs shared workspaces, one of the tools above will suit you better.

## How do I start without logging in?

- Add RequestFox from the Chrome Web Store or Firefox Add-ons. There's no sign-up step.

- Press Compose in the top bar, type an address, and press Send.

- Already have a collection? In Compose open Import and press Import a collection…. It reads Postman, Insomnia, Bruno, Hoppscotch and Thunder Client exports, and HAR files. How to import a Postman collection.

# A Postman Interceptor alternative: record your web app's API calls in the browser

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/postman-interceptor-alternative.html

Postman Interceptor is a browser extension that captures requests and cookies and hands them to Postman, so Postman has to be running (the desktop app) or open (the web app) [1]. RequestFox is another browser extension, for Chrome, Edge and Firefox. It records the calls a web app makes and flags the broken ones inside the browser, with no other app, and exports a Postman collection when you want the calls in Postman.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026. Facts about Postman are from its own documentation, checked 4 November 2026; sources below. Written by the RequestFox team.

## What does Postman Interceptor do, and what does it need?

Postman's documentation describes Interceptor as a companion to Postman that captures API traffic, including requests and cookies, from a web browser [1]. In short:

- You start a capture session, use your browser, and stop it. The session then opens in Postman, where you can read its requests and cookies, and save the requests to a collection, grouped in folders by domain, by endpoint or both [1].

- You can limit a capture by method and by domain or address, with regular expressions [1].

- It can also sync cookies from the browser to the Postman cookie jar [1].

- It needs Postman: the message "Interceptor disconnected" means the Postman desktop app is not running or the Postman web app is not open. Postman also asks that you are in an internal workspace where you can edit [1].

- On Linux, and on older Postman versions for macOS and Windows, it needs a helper called Interceptor Bridge [1].

- The extension is available for Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Edge [1].

## How is RequestFox different?

|

| | RequestFox | Postman Interceptor

| What it is | A browser extension with its own side panel in Chrome and sidebar in Firefox | A browser extension that works with Postman [1]

| Needs another app | No. The log is in the panel | Postman, running or open, and a workspace you can edit [1]

| Where recorded calls go | Its own log, kept in History on your device | Into Postman, as a session in its History [1]

| What it does with them | Flags failed, slow, duplicate and retried calls, N+1 bursts and errors inside a 200 OK; replay, mock, check, export | Lists requests and cookies, with graphs of traffic by method, domain or content type [1]

| Cookies | Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields are redacted by default in what you view or export | Captures cookies and can sync them to the Postman cookie jar [1]

| Into Postman | Export a Postman collection file, then import it | Built in: the session opens in Postman [1]

## Which one should I pick?

- Interceptor fits when you already work in Postman and want captured calls to land in its collections, in a workspace you share, or need its cookie sync.

- RequestFox fits when you are testing a web app and want the broken calls found for you, in the browser, with nothing else to run and no account.

- You can use both. RequestFox imports and exports Postman collections, so a recording can end up in Postman. RequestFox vs Postman compares the two tools as a whole.

## How do I record calls with RequestFox and open them in Postman?

### Record the calls in RequestFox

Open the site, open RequestFox and press Start Recording (or Alt Shift S), then use the site as usual. Press Stop when you have the flow. How to record API calls.

### Export a Postman collection

Press Export (bottom right) and choose Postman collection. The file is a Postman Collection v2.1. Postman's import page says its old v1 collection format is no longer supported [2].

### Import it in Postman

In Postman, choose Use resources or import, open the Import tab and pick the file [2]. The collection appears in your sidebar.

What RequestFox records stays in your browser, and nothing is sent to us. The exported file goes where you put it. Interceptor passes what it captures to Postman, encrypted [1].

## What does RequestFox not do?

- It runs in Chrome, Edge and Firefox only.

- It does not put recorded calls into a Postman workspace by itself: you export a file and import it.

- It does not sync the browser's cookies to Postman. Cookie values are never exported or logged.

- There is no team workspace or cloud sync. Share work as files, such as collections and reports.

- It sees what a browser tab sends. Mobile and desktop apps need a proxy tool such as HTTP Toolkit, Proxyman or Charles.

## Sources

- Postman Docs, "Capture traffic from a web browser using Postman Interceptor". Checked 4 November 2026. learning.postman.com

- Postman Docs, "Import data into Postman". Checked 4 November 2026. learning.postman.com

# See how clients really call your API

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/use-api-developers.html

RequestFox records what a real web client sends to your API, checks every call against your OpenAPI spec, flags responses whose shape changed, and turns that traffic into requests, checks, CI runs and load tests, all from the browser.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

Live calls checked against your spec.

## Catch drift between the spec and what ships

Link your OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 spec: calls that break it show “Spec mismatch” with the reason, undocumented calls show “Not in spec”, and coverage counts the operations a test touched. Without a spec, Schema changed still marks a response whose JSON shape changed. How to check against OpenAPI.

## Send, chain and sign

Compose with environments and secret variables, chain values from one response into the next request, and sign with OAuth 2.0, AWS Signature v4 or an HMAC preset. Import your Postman, Insomnia, Bruno or Hoppscotch collections, or the spec itself, from a file, a folder or a URL, and export collections back out for Bruno, Insomnia or Hoppscotch. Send QUERY requests, sign in with OAuth device code, call SOAP services from a WSDL, or send gRPC-Web and Connect from your own .proto files.

## Load tests from real traffic

Performance turns a recording into a k6, JMeter, Gatling or Locust script, with each endpoint's measured p95 latency as its pass/fail threshold. The command-line tool has its own local load test too. How to run checks in CI.

## Passive security checks

Every response is read for problems such as a token in a URL query, a JWT with alg "none", wildcard CORS with credentials, or card numbers in a response, and flagged Security. These checks only read what was recorded; nothing extra is sent.

## A worked example: a price that became a string

Say you link your OpenAPI spec and click through the staging app. GET /api/products/42 comes back 200, and the page looks fine, but the card shows Spec mismatch. Details says the response body's price was a string where the spec expects a number. Another call shows Not in spec: the app uses an endpoint the spec does not describe. Press "Why is this flagged?" for the next step: Details names each place; fix the API or the spec.

The Spec coverage line counts how many of the spec's operations this session called, for example 3 of 6, so you also see what no one has exercised yet. To keep the check, export the session as JSON and run the command-line tool's conform against the spec in CI: it exits with 1 on a mismatch, so the build fails when the shape drifts again. How to check against OpenAPI.

## Point it at your staging app.

Add to Chrome, free
Add to Firefox

# Debug the API calls your UI makes

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/use-frontend-developers.html

RequestFox shows every call your app makes with the click and the page functions behind it, flags double fetches, N+1 bursts and slow endpoints, and lets you mock loading, empty and error states in place. It runs beside your app, in the browser you already debug in.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

The Timeline: what fired, when, and how long it took.

## Why did that call fire?

Every call is tied to the click or form submit that caused it. Details shows "Called from", the page functions that made it, plus the timing split (DNS, connect, TLS, waiting, download).

## Find wasted calls

- Duplicate · after 140 ms the same request twice in a moment, often an effect that runs twice.

- One call per item N+1: a call for each item in a list, where one batched call would do.

- Performance lists the heaviest endpoints; the Timeline shows what waited on what.

## See every UI state without touching the backend

Mock an empty list, an error, a slow response or a dropped connection, then check your loading, empty and error screens. Need to change a call in flight? Pause it with a breakpoint and edit it on the way. How to mock an API response.

## GraphQL, streams and sockets

GraphQL calls are told apart by operation, and errors inside a 200 OK are flagged. Load the schema and recorded calls are checked against it. Server-sent events and token streams (read with fetch, XMLHttpRequest or EventSource) show their events live, with error events, a missing end marker and long pauses flagged, and WebSocket frames are listed with the calls. To see how a page copes, rewrite a response with a script or slow the whole tab down (both Chrome), or make an endpoint fail with a mock set that stays on.

## A worked example: a search box that asks twice

Say you type "boots" into a search box and the results flicker. In RequestFox, GET /api/search?q=boots shows twice, and the second card carries Duplicate · after 140 ms. Press "Why is this flagged?": "The same call was made again within moments: often a double click or a double render." Its next step: make the page send the call once, and use Repeats on the card to see each copy and what started it.

Open Details on one copy: "Called from" lists the page functions that made the call, so you know where to look in your code. Often it's an effect that runs twice. Fix it and search again: one card means the double fetch is gone. Want to see how the results list looks while the response is slow? Mock a slow response for that endpoint.

## Debug your next feature with it.

Add to Chrome, free
Add to Firefox

# Catch the API bugs the screen hides

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/use-qa-testers.html

RequestFox is a free browser extension that lets a manual tester test an API without writing code: press Start, use the app as a user would, watch the flags, and copy a bug report from the call that went wrong. A page can look fine while a call behind it failed, fired twice or returned an error inside a 200 OK. RequestFox flags those as they happen and ties each one to your click.

For RequestFox 2.5.0, checked 19 November 2026.

Every session is kept in History.

## How to test an API without code

- Open the RequestFox side panel on the page you're testing and press Start.

- Use the app the way a user would. Every call is listed the moment it starts.

- Watch the flags on the calls. Press "Why is this flagged?" for the reason in plain words and a next step.

- On the call that went wrong, open More and choose Copy bug report, or open a GitHub or Linear issue from it (set up once in Settings).

## What you will find that the screen does not show

- Calls that failed quietly while the page kept a stale value.

- The same request sent twice by one click (a double submit), or retried after a failure.

- A GraphQL or JSON-RPC error inside a 200 OK.

- A 401 caused by an expired token, said in words.

- A response whose shape changed since earlier in the session.

- JavaScript errors, next to the calls.

How to record API calls.

## A worked example: an order that "worked"

Say you test a shop. You press Place order and the page shows a green "Order placed" message. In RequestFox, POST /api/orders carries the Failed flag and HTTP 500, and the card is tied to the click that sent it. Press "Why is this flagged?" and it says: "The server failed while answering (a 5xx status)." Its next step: check the server's logs for that moment, and press Replay to send the same request again and see whether it repeats. In a long session, type status:500 in the search box to list only the calls that failed that way.

Then choose Copy bug report from More on that call, or open the GitHub or Linear issue from it. The developer gets the call itself, with its status, instead of "the order sometimes fails". You didn't write code or open DevTools.

## Bug reports nobody has to reproduce

Open a GitHub or Linear issue from a call with the repro filled in, or export the session as a self-contained HTML report or a HAR file to attach. Authorization headers, cookies and secret-shaped fields are redacted by default, so the evidence is safe to share as it is.

## Test the edge cases without waiting for the backend

Make an endpoint fail, drag or return an empty list, and see what the page does. Calls you changed are labelled, so nobody files them as real bugs by mistake. How to mock an API response.

## Make a manual check repeatable

Save the calls that matter, add pass/fail checks, chain them into a suite, and hand the suite to CI. How to run API checks in CI.

## Try it on your next test run.

Add to Chrome, free
Add to Firefox

# Privacy policy

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/privacy.html

RequestFox is a developer tool for Chrome, Edge and Firefox that watches and tests API traffic during manual QA. It does not collect, transmit, or sell any data. It has no server of its own, no analytics, no telemetry and no account.

Last updated: 17 November 2026

## 1. What RequestFox stores

Everything it records (network requests and responses, console messages, WebSocket frames, optional screenshots) and everything you save (settings, collections, environments, sessions, saved WebSocket messages) lives only in your browser's own local storage and IndexedDB, on your own machine. A recording of a private (incognito) window is the one exception: it is kept in memory only, never written to disk or to History, so export it before you close the window. If you choose Link a folder… (Chrome), your saved requests, environments, suites, checks and rules are also written as files to the folder you pick, and kept up to date there. Passwords, tokens and keys RequestFox recognises are written as {{placeholders}}, not their values. You can delete any session, or all of them, at any time from the extension. Authorization headers, cookies and fields that look like secrets are redacted by default in everything RequestFox keeps, shows in its log or exports; only Compose shows the response to your own request as it came, and does not keep it in the log. Compose's Recent list keeps your last 100 Compose and saved-request sends with their responses on this device (in the browser's IndexedDB), redacted the way the log is (a typed Auth token, password or key is never kept there), until you press Clear under Recent. A response you keep with Save as example stays on that saved request as it came, apart from cookies and Authorization headers, on this device only; the copies you share (Export workspace or Export to Postman without credentials, and a linked folder) replace values that look like secrets with {{placeholders}}. The responses the "Same response as last time" check keeps are stored on this device with tokens, keys and session ids replaced by «scrubbed» before they are written. The unredacted copy needed to replay a request is kept only in memory and the browser's session storage, which is never written to disk, is readable only by the extension, and is cleared when the browser closes. If you turn on the cookie jar for a site (Settings, Cookie jar), the cookies that site sets in responses to the requests RequestFox sends itself, and any you add by hand or import from the browser, are kept on this device: those with an expiry in the browser's local storage until they expire or you clear them, session cookies only in the browser's session storage, which is never written to disk and is cleared when the browser closes. Their values never go into an export, a linked folder, code, History, Recent, a report or the log; Clear the jar deletes them all. While Slow down the whole tab (Chrome) is on, the tab's id and title and the speed you picked are kept in the browser's session storage, and removed when it goes off. MCP control keeps only whether it is switched on and the port you typed; its session key lives only in the panel's memory, and the list of MCP actions is kept in the browser's session storage, which is never written to disk, until the browser closes.

## 2. Requests you send

RequestFox sends a network request only when you ask it to. Compose & Send, Replay and test suites send the request you built or recorded to the URL in it, with the headers and body you set. With nothing recording, Compose & Send, a saved request's Send and the steps of a test suite you run go from the extension itself, to the same URL and without any page's cookies; the browser first asks you to allow those sites, unless you already did. If you turn on the cookie jar for a site, those requests to that site also carry the cookies the jar holds for it, and the cookies its responses set go into the jar; the browser's own cookies are still neither sent nor changed. If you set up an OAuth 2.0 sign-in, the browser's sign-in window opens at the provider's authorization URL, and the token exchange goes to the token URL you entered. "Fill from issuer" reads the OpenID Connect discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration) from the issuer address you entered. Import from a URL reads the OpenAPI, collection or WSDL file at the address you type, without cookies, and the schema files a WSDL links to; for a file on another site the browser asks you first. The MCP server tester sends the requests you pick (list tools, call one, read a resource) to the server address you type; a server's request for a model completion is declined. If that server asks you to sign in and you press Sign in…, RequestFox reads the sign-in addresses the server publishes, registers itself with that sign-in server (it sends the name RequestFox and its own redirect address, nothing about you), opens the browser's sign-in window there, and sends the token request to the address that sign-in server names. The sign-in is then kept in Settings like one you set up yourself. MCP control, off until you turn it on (Settings, Sign-in, cookies & connections, MCP control), connects the panel to the RequestFox MCP server that you start yourself on this computer (it is inside the one-file RequestFox command-line tool, requestfox-ci.mjs, which MCP control lets you download), at http://127.0.0.1 on the port you type, after you type the one-time pairing code it prints; it reaches nothing else. An AI agent you run can then ask RequestFox, through that server, to start or stop recording, read or clear the calls in the log, replay one, send a request from the extension (without any page's cookies or the cookie jar's) wherever your site access reaches, which after Start Recording is every site and after Connect every port on 127.0.0.1, add, change or delete mock and fail rules, switch rule sets and mock sets on or off, run saved requests and test suites, delete a saved collection, export a HAR file, a report or the API docs, or slow down a tab once you have allowed the debugger permission yourself. Each action is listed in the panel under MCP actions. What goes back to the agent is redacted the way exports are, and it never gets the cookie jar, the vault, secret variables or OAuth tokens. A request the agent writes itself gets no {{variables}} filled in, so no secret variable or OAuth token can be sent where it asks; a saved request or suite it runs goes to its own saved address, as its Send does. RequestFox waits for your click before it deletes or clears anything, before it changes a rule you made, before every request the agent writes or replays (it shows you the address), and before a saved request or suite whose method changes data; a request to the server's own port is refused. The link itself sends nothing off this computer; what the agent does with the responses is up to that agent. In plain words: with MCP control on, what RequestFox observes is handed, redacted, to the program you paired on this computer, which may send it elsewhere. The link ends when you press Disconnect, close the panel or quit the browser, and after 8 hours at most. The WebSocket client connects to the address you type; in Socket.IO mode it sends the auth payload you entered to that server. A GraphQL subscription in Compose opens the browser's WebSocket to the endpoint you typed, with the request's headers and auth in its first message and, once you allow that site, with its opening handshake. If the page you test cannot reach an API on another origin, Compose can send the request from the extension instead, after you click "Send from the extension instead"; it goes to the same URL, without the page's cookies. After you choose a site this way, your later Compose sends and test-suite steps to that site also go from the extension until the browser closes, and Replay of a request sent this way goes the same way. A GET, HEAD or OPTIONS Replay that the page's CORS rules block is sent again from the extension by itself, the same way; any other method offers "Replay from the extension" first. The "Security probe (OPTIONS)" action asks you to confirm first, then sends one OPTIONS request to that request's own address. "Open GitHub issue" and "Open Linear issue" open your GitHub or Linear page in a new tab with the issue text in the link. None of these go to RequestFox or to anyone it works with, because there is no such party. They go to the servers you named, which see them as they would see any request from your browser.

## 3. Host access

Access to websites is optional and requested only when you press Start Recording, or, for the sites involved, when you send a request from Compose or run a test suite with nothing recording, or switch on a rule set or a mock set, or turn on the cookie jar for a site, or import from a URL, connect to an MCP server or sign in to one, at an address on a site not yet allowed. It is used to observe the network traffic of the tabs you record (by default the tabs of the recorded window that show the site you started the recording on, or every tab of that window if you tick "Record every tab in this window, whatever site it shows" in Settings, What gets recorded), for the features described in the store listing, and, when you choose "Send from the extension instead" or send from Compose or run a test suite with nothing recording, to send your request to that site from the extension (section 2). While a recording is running, the recording scripts load in every tab, but report only from the tabs you record (section 6, scripting). What it observes there never leaves your device. The one exception is MCP control (section 2): while it is on, what an AI agent asks for is handed, redacted, to the program you paired on this computer, and that program may send it elsewhere. Once allowed, that access stays after you stop recording, until you remove it in your browser's settings for the extension. You can also give it back in Settings (Privacy & evidence, Give access back), which first stops the recording and switches off the rule sets and mock sets kept on without recording. A rule set you switch on (Settings, Mocks and rules, Header and URL rules, Keep some rules on without recording) uses this same access, only for the sites you named: it changes headers or addresses of requests to those sites, in every tab and with nothing recording, until you switch it off. A mock set you switch on (Settings, Mocks and rules, Mock or break an endpoint, Keep some mocks on without recording) uses this same access, only for the sites you named: on the pages of those sites it answers the calls that match its rules with the mock response, error or delay you set, in every tab and with nothing recording, until you switch it off. It records nothing there. The cookie jar uses this same access, only for the sites you turn it on for: it adds the jar's cookies to RequestFox's own requests to those sites and reads the cookies their responses set. MCP control asks for this same access for http://127.0.0.1 only, when you press Connect, and uses it only to reach that RequestFox MCP server on this computer. RequestFox never asks for site access or any other permission for an MCP client; an action that needs one works only when you have already allowed it.

## 4. OAuth tokens

Tokens from an OAuth 2.0 sign-in, the client secrets of your sign-ins and your secret variables are encrypted (AES-GCM) before they are written to browser storage. The decryption key is held only in memory and in the browser's session storage, which is never written to disk, and is never sent anywhere. It is cleared when you lock the vault, when the vault has not been used for the time you choose (15 minutes unless you change it in Settings), or when the browser closes, and you then enter the passphrase again.

## 5. No AI

RequestFox contains no AI model and no AI code. RequestFox gives nothing you record, type or send to any AI service, and no model runs in the extension. Everything it does with your requests is ordinary code that runs on your device. MCP control (section 2), off until you turn it on, lets an AI agent that you run yourself, outside RequestFox, ask RequestFox for actions over a link on this computer; the redacted responses go to that agent, and what it does with them (for example, sending them to its own AI service) is up to the agent you chose.

## 6. Permissions

RequestFox asks for these browser permissions, each only for the job named:

- scripting: while a recording is running, register the recording scripts for all sites, so they load in every tab that opens or reloads in that time, in any window, and add them to the tabs you record that were already open. Only in the tabs you record do they report what the page's calls send and receive, its console messages and the clicks that led to a call. In every other tab they report nothing: a page's first calls are kept in that page's own memory (at most 200 calls or 2 MB) until RequestFox answers that the tab is not recorded, at most 20 seconds, and are then dropped. They are removed when the recording stops, so a page loaded after that gets none; a page that already has them keeps them, idle, until it reloads. For a mock set you switch on, the same scripts go into the pages of the sites you named, where they answer the matching calls with your mock, error or delay, and record nothing.

- webRequest: read request and response details (method, address, headers, request body, status, timing, and a WebSocket's opening handshake) of the tabs you record, while a recording is running; and, for RequestFox's own requests, the cookies set in responses from a site whose cookie jar is on and, when you turn off Follow redirects for a request, the status and address of the redirect.

- declarativeNetRequestWithHostAccess: apply the header-override and URL-rewrite rules that you define yourself in Settings, while recording and, for a rule set you switch on, with nothing recording, and add the cookie jar's cookies to RequestFox's own requests to a site you turned the jar on for; and, on RequestFox's own requests only, set the headers you typed in Compose that a browser request cannot carry (Cookie, Origin, Referer, User-Agent, Accept-Encoding) and the headers you typed for the WebSocket client or a GraphQL subscription, which go with its opening handshake. It acts only on sites you have given RequestFox access to.

- storage and unlimitedStorage: keep your settings, collections and sessions on your device; the second lets long recordings be saved without hitting the browser's default storage limit.

- tabs: read the address and title of the tabs you record and of the tab in front, and open reports and links in a new tab.

- downloads (optional, asked at your first export): save the exports you ask for (HAR, reports, scripts) as files. Without it, the file is saved through a download link instead.

- notifications: show a desktop alert when a recording sees an error or a changed response shape. You can turn this off in Settings.

- identity: open the OAuth sign-in window for a sign-in you set up, or one you start with Sign in… in the MCP server tester.

- sidePanel (Chrome): show RequestFox in the browser's side panel. Firefox uses its own sidebar and needs no permission for it.

- <all_urls> (optional host access): requested when you press Start Recording, or for the sites involved when you send from Compose or run a test suite with nothing recording, or switch on a rule set or a mock set, or turn on the cookie jar for a site, or import from a URL, connect to an MCP server or sign in to one, at an address on a site not yet allowed, so Chrome or Firefox asks you first; Send from the extension instead uses the same access, and MCP control asks for it for http://127.0.0.1 only, when you press Connect. With Take a screenshot when a call is flagged switched on (Settings, Privacy & evidence; off by default), the same access lets RequestFox take a picture of the recorded tab, when it is the tab in front, as a call in it is flagged or the page logs an error. See section 3.

- debugger (optional, Chrome only): requested only the first time you turn on Slow down the whole tab (Settings), after RequestFox has said that Chrome then shows its own "started debugging this browser" bar. It is used only to set the network conditions (a slower speed, or offline) of the one tab you pick. Chrome applies network conditions only while the DevTools protocol's Network domain is enabled, so RequestFox sends Network.enable, Network.emulateNetworkConditions and Network.disable and no other command; it does not listen to, read or store the events this produces, and reads nothing from the tab. It lets the tab go when you turn it off, stop recording, close the tab or the last open RequestFox panel, or close Chrome's bar. Firefox has no such permission, so this does not appear there.

- cookies (optional): requested only when you press Import from this browser in the cookie jar, together with access to that one site, so Chrome or Firefox asks you first. It is used then, to read the browser's own cookies for that site and copy them into the jar; RequestFox never changes or deletes the browser's cookies.

## 7. Third parties

Since RequestFox collects no data, it shares none. Requests you send (section 2) reach the servers you chose, nothing more. With MCP control on, the redacted responses to what a connected AI agent asks for go to that agent (section 2).

## 8. Changes and contact

We may update this policy from time to time; changes will appear on this page with a new date. Questions about this policy or the extension's behavior: email requestfox10304@gmail.com.

## Check it yourself

You do not have to take this page on trust. Everything RequestFox runs is in the package you installed, and you can read it and watch it.

- Read the code. The extension's .js files are the compiled TypeScript, not minified, and the command-line tool is one readable file. They leave out the source code's comments, so the panel opens faster; every line of code is there, with its own names. In Chrome, open chrome://extensions, turn on Developer mode and note RequestFox's ID: its files are in your browser profile's Extensions folder under that ID. In Firefox the add-on is one .xpi file, a zip you can open, in the extensions folder of your profile (about:support, Profile Folder).

- Watch what it sends. In Chrome, chrome://extensions with Developer mode on: under RequestFox, Inspect views, service worker, then the Network tab; right-click inside the side panel and choose Inspect for the panel's own requests. In Firefox, about:debugging, This Firefox, RequestFox, Inspect. You will see only the requests you send (section 2), and nothing to us.

- Check a download. Each release lists the SHA-256 of its two store packages and of requestfox-ci.mjs, the command-line tool, in its changelog entry. The stores sign their packages on the way, so a package downloaded from a store is not the uploaded one byte for byte, and no list of the files inside is published. The file you can check is the requestfox-ci.mjs the panel hands out: its SHA-256 (sha256sum on Linux and macOS, Get-FileHash on Windows) must be the one in the list.

The source repository is not public; the code that runs is the code you can read here.

## Nothing to sign up for. Nothing sent to us.

Free, in Chrome and Firefox.

Add to Chrome, free
Add to Firefox

# Changelog

Address: https://requestfox.accessisight.com/changelog.html

What changed in the newest RequestFox releases, newest first. This page is built from the project's own changelog, so it says exactly what shipped. The current version is 2.5.0.

## 2.5.0 19 November 2026

In short. Mock is a button on every call: press it, change the response, press Mock it. Settings opens on Mocks & rules and every screen shows less at first. Secrets are hidden in more places, and an export that still holds one asks first.

### New for you in this release

- After you install, one welcome page says where the panel is (the toolbar icon; in Chrome, pin it from the puzzle menu) and the three steps to start. It opens once, never on an update.
- The first screen asks for nothing but Start Recording: the session name and the reload option wait under Options.
- A recording covers the tab you start it on, wherever it goes (a sign-in on another site included), and the other tabs of that window while they show the same site. To record every tab of the window, tick Record every tab in this window, whatever site it shows in Settings, What gets recorded.
- After Stop a mock says Mock paused and answers again at the next recording; Delete mock removes it, and one All rules switch pauses every rule at once.
- Help keeps its tours short; behind All tours it now has What's new in 2.5 and Report a problem…, which opens your own mail program with three questions, or copies a short diagnostics text, and sends nothing itself.
- Open in a tab (Help, More help) opens the whole panel in a browser tab. There, in a wide window, Compose shows the response beside the request, and the log starts as the table.
- The command-line tool reads an environment variable only when you allow it (--allow-env NAME); without it, a config that reads one stops with one sentence that names the flag (exit 2). It also carries the MCP server (node requestfox-ci.mjs mcp), so a store install has it: Settings, MCP control, Download the CLI.

### Mocking

- Mock is a button on every request card, next to Replay, not an item at the bottom of its ··· menu. It opens a dialog that holds the response the server sent: change the Status (200 to 599) or the Body, then press Mock it. A call that got no response (the backend is down) starts as 200 with {}. Reload the page or repeat the action to see the mocked response.
- The card then says Mocked. Its menu edits the response, keeps the mock on without recording, turns it off or deletes it; a mock that is off says Mock off, with Turn on. More options… in the dialog opens the full rule in Settings with what you typed, and Keep it on without recording… saves it into a mock set for that site.
- A mock made from a call answers that address and only that one: past cache-busters (_=, and t= or ts= only with a made-up value), a hidden query value (a redacted ?key= stands for any value), a redirected call (the address the page asked for), a page with <base href>, a call the page makes while it loads, and a reload after the browser let the extension sleep. It wins over an older, broader rule. A GraphQL mock answers only its operation, persisted queries included.
- Match has Pattern with \* (/api/users/* answers every user), and a mock can wait before it answers (Delay ms). The rule editor shows a mock's GraphQL operation, its Content type and the recorded headers it sends back; a status outside 200 to 599 is refused, and a body that is not JSON is flagged.
- Replay and Compose always call the real server, and the card says so ("Not mocked"). A call a mock should have answered says why it was not: the mock is off (with Turn on), the page called before RequestFox was ready, or the page did not make the call itself. Page files and EventSource streams, which a mock cannot answer, have no Mock or Block.
- A mocked response reads like a real one: a synchronous XMLHttpRequest gets it at once, with the status text, responseURL, the page's responseType and progress events; a HEAD response has no body.
- Mocks on (n) counts only the rules that can reach this recording. Mock and break rules go only to the tabs you record, and Stop clears them.
- Mock sets keep their exact addresses through export and import. The workspace export asks before it writes secrets held in mock rules. MCP create_rule and update_rule take match: "exact", and editing a mock made from a card keeps its address and GraphQL operation.
- A new rule mode, Change the response: the real call goes out and the page gets the response with one text or JSON field replaced ($.price). No script, so it works in Firefox too, and in mock sets.
- A script rule can Respond without calling the server: the script writes the whole response and the real server is never asked.
- Mock the calls shown in the log… (under the mock sets) makes one exact mock for each call the log shows, with its newest response, in one new mock set that is off until you turn it on. A rule's row says how many calls of this recording it answered.
- A mock can answer Only when the request body contains a text or a JSON field ($.method = getUser), so one JSON-RPC address can have a mock per action. Load the body from a file… fills the Body, and a mock made from an image or other bytes answers with those bytes.
- A mock's Response headers are rows you can edit, add and remove; a header no page can read (Set-Cookie) or a name a browser cannot send is refused by name. The response breakpoint now pauses XMLHttpRequest responses too, and its Headers box changes the response's headers.
- Find a rule appears once you have ten rules. Compare anyway makes a rule compare a query value it would otherwise ignore because it changes on every call (?from= with a time).
- Esc in a breakpoint now lets the paused call go on unchanged (it used to abort it); only Abort stops it, and once you have changed something Esc asks you to press Resume or Abort.
- Closing Settings with a rule or a set half typed asks Save what you typed? first. Save and keep on saves a mock set and switches it on in one step.

### Easier screens

- Settings opens on Mocks & rules, and its rows come in the order people need them: Mocks & rules, Appearance, Notifications, What gets recorded (was Noise filters), Privacy & evidence, When to flag a call (was Detection thresholds), Full, Background or Mini (was Panel mode), and a new last row, Sign-in, cookies & connections (OAuth 2.0 and the vault, the cookie jar, the issue tracker, MCP control).
- Mock sets and header-rule sets sit inside the group whose rules they keep on, under Keep some mocks on without recording and Keep some rules on without recording, and are called sets; saved threshold sets sit in When to flag a call. An OAuth 2.0 profile is now a sign-in, everywhere you read it.
- A Settings group opens on one short line per hint, with the rest under More about this. The vault passphrase waits behind Vault passphrase… until it is needed. Each switch says On or Keep on beside it. Nothing shows under the Done bar, and Settings never scrolls sideways.
- The live log starts higher: "9 calls" on one line, two or more repeated problems fold into Repeated problems: N, and each one says it once, in words ("GET /api/data · failed 3×"). The table's sort hint shows only until the first sort.
- A failed call's card opens on why it failed: its Response, else its Details. Overview rows carry their finding codes in the tooltip only.
- After Stop, one quiet line says the session is over and what it kept. Over an open panel, the start bar is one slim row with a quiet Start.
- The card menu says Copy as cURL, and Edit and send again… comes before Open in Compose. The search box says "Search calls, e.g. 500 or /login", and its help button is Search tips.
- The first-run tour is three plain slides that name Replay and Mock. Help opens on a short list, How to mock a call among them; the rest wait behind All tours.
- At 480 px and wider, Compose, History and Timeline carry a short word in the top bar.
- Compose: the response says its status once, with Hex and Save as example under ···; the five tabs fit one row (measured in ten languages). Long hints are one short line, and an auth field never repeats its label as a placeholder. Performance opens on Summary, then Slowest endpoints, and its five tiles read 3 + 2 at 360 px. An empty suite shows only how to add a step.

### Privacy

- A recording of a private (incognito) window is kept in memory only: it is never written to disk or to History, and one line in the recording bar says so ("Private window: this recording is not saved. Export it before you close the window.").
- One set of redaction rules for every path: the log, History, HAR, the report, CSV, Postman, Copy as cURL, a bug report and the files you share. It now also hides form and multipart fields (user[password]=), numbers under card, CVV, OTP or PIN names, XML and SOAP values, HTML hidden inputs, GraphQL arguments, Bearer tokens and JWTs anywhere in a text, user:pass@ in an address, and the secrets in Location, Link and Referer addresses. Thirteen credential headers are hidden by name.
- History → Open file hides the tokens, passwords and cookies in a HAR or session file, as your Redact setting says. Playwright, Cypress and issue titles carry no query values.
- Exporting a session that still holds secrets asks first: Export with secrets hidden (the default) or Export as it is. The export offered at Stop always hides them.
- An OAuth client secret is kept encrypted in the vault, not in plain storage.
- Cookies imported from the browser into the cookie jar stay in memory until the browser closes, unless you tick Keep imported cookies after the browser closes for that site.
- A click's label never holds what was typed in a field. An alert about a call is shown in full only in that call's tab. No raw ?access_token= address is written to disk while redaction is on, and the background logs no call addresses.
- The page script reads the extension's messages through a getter it keeps from the start, so a page cannot read them by patching the browser.
- The privacy policy says what the recording scripts do while recording (they load in every tab and report only from the tabs you record), that webRequest reads the request body, and that the opt-in screenshot uses the site access. Its contact address is in section 8.

### Client

- A suite step whose status check expects an error (status = 404, say) passes when the server sends that status; before, any 4xx or 5xx failed the step. The panel and the CLI judge it the same way.
- A Postman, Insomnia, Bruno or Hoppscotch file with folders imports as a folder of collections, one per folder. Import as one flat list instead, in the dialog that ends the import, brings it in as one collection.
- A folder's ··· menu has Run as a suite… and Export…: the whole imported file runs as one suite, or goes back out to Postman, Bruno, Insomnia or Hoppscotch as one file with its folders.
- A curl command pasted into Compose's address fills the method, address, headers and body.
- A new vault passphrase is typed twice, and Forgot the passphrase? says what can be done.
- A suite run's result rows open to every check with what it got, and have Open the response and Copy results.
- Under Compose's address a line says where the request goes (Sends to …) or which variable the environment lacks (Not set in “Staging”: id).
- Bruno and Thunder Client assertions come in as checks.
- A suite's data table can be pasted from Excel (tabs, or ;) or be a JSON file, and a data-driven run works with no environment too.
- Two changes in how a request is sent: a JSON body with no Content-Type header goes out as application/json (Compose says "Sent as …" under the body; add a Content-Type header to change it); and a request's Auth can be From the collection, while No auth now means no auth is sent, even when the collection has one.
- Follow redirects (on by default): off, a request stops at a redirect and shows its status and Location. Time limit (s) in Advanced stops a request that takes too long, and says so; empty means no limit.
- A File body sends one file as the whole body (up to 15 MB).
- Cookie, Origin, Referer, User-Agent and Accept-Encoding headers you type are sent as typed, on RequestFox's own requests.
- Importing a collection says what was Not kept, and an import over an existing collection can replace it (the old one goes to Recently deleted); Insomnia environment variables come along.
- OAuth 2.0 is in Compose's Auth list: pick a saved sign-in and Compose sends its token; with none saved, Set up a sign-in… opens the form. Collection and folder settings offer it too.
- Send on a saved row opens that request, then sends it. Closing a changed request offers Save and close, and so does opening a sixth request while the oldest has changes.
- A 4xx or 5xx response is never shown in success green, also for a send an MCP client started. A response with no body says "No body.", and the link after a send reads Save request….
- A trip from Compose into Settings comes back to Compose. "Recently deleted" closes again, a URL the panel fills in reads from its start, and the linked line's Unlink says "Stop using its settings".
- A Form (URL-encoded) body fills each {{variable}}, then encodes it: a password or client secret with +, & or % goes out as typed, in Compose, a saved request's Send and a suite step.
- An address with no http:// (localhost:3000/api) gets it, and the address box shows what is sent; a path alone with nothing recording says to write the whole address.
- A request kept over a reload says when it still holds *REDACTED*, and Send stops there (with Send anyway). Its saved header and token come back from the saved request, so Save changes keeps them.
- A {{name}} that came with a recorded call (the log, a past session, a HAR) or a link in a response is the page's text: Send leaves it as text, so a page can no longer have your variables or vault secrets filled in and sent to it. The status line names them, with Fill with my values.

### Protocols

- WebSocket: up to 5 connections at once, headers for the opening handshake (with the server's response under Show headers), Socket.IO v2 as well as v3 and v4, binary messages sent from hex or saved as a file, Copy on one message, Copy log, Socket.IO binary arguments ({"$binary": "…"}), and saved WebSocket requests.
- gRPC: error details decoded, live stream rows, "Fields of" a message (nested ones too), Show default values, the loaded .proto files under Files (n) with one × each, and grpcurl and buf commands under Copy as code.
- SOAP: a SOAP Fault shown as one, rpc/encoded services, and WS-Security (UsernameToken) in the Auth list.
- MCP server tester: Sign in… when a server asks for it, a server's question (elicitation) answered with a form under The server asks, with Decline, the older HTTP+SSE transport, resource templates, and a check of a tool's result against its output schema.
- GraphQL: subscriptions over SSE as well as WebSocket (over WebSocket, their headers go with the handshake too), and three more checks on a query before it is sent.
